parts.title: From the Tropics Toward the Arctic: How Male and Female Flowers Are Arranged on Trees and Shrubs in Northern Hemisphere Forests, and What Drives the Pattern
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

Every flowering plant has a "sexual system": a way of arranging its male and female flower parts. This is one of the key traits shaping how communities of woody plants (trees and shrubs) live and evolve. Even so, we still know too little about how these systems change from warm, wet places to cold or dry ones.

Methods

We gathered information on 3,595 kinds of trees and shrubs from 30 large forest plots. Scientists have mapped and tracked every tree in these plots for many years. The plots stretch across tropical, subtropical and temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere. To find large-scale patterns, we used three statistical tools. Linear regression tests whether one thing rises or falls steadily as another changes. Redundancy analysis checks how well a set of environmental conditions explains differences among communities. Structural equation modeling maps how several factors might connect to one another, both directly and indirectly.

Results

Monoecious species carry separate male and female flowers on the same plant. Their share of the species in a forest rose as we moved north, away from the equator. Dioecious species have male and female flowers on different plants, and their share fell. The two groups therefore showed opposite trends. Climate, especially temperature and rainfall, was the main driver of these patterns. The link between climate and sexual systems was stronger in trees than in shrubs.

Discussion

These results show that the way woody plant sexual systems vary from place to place is closely tied to changes in climate. Monoecious and dioecious species shifted consistently as conditions changed. This points to the real ecological importance of sexual systems. It also suggests they may offer useful, trait-based clues about how forest communities respond to a changing environment. Further long-term studies are needed to judge whether they could help track forests as the climate keeps changing.

Keywords: climate change, ecological indicator, change with latitude, sexual systems, woody plants
parts.introduction_first:
One of the biggest patterns in the living world is that the number of species drops as you travel from the equator toward the poles. We can see this pattern in forests across many different climate zones (Rosenzweig, 1995).

Flowers are a plant's sexual organs, part of how it reproduces. Botanists sort plants' sexual systems into several types, including female-monoecious and dioecious systems, along with some more complex arrangements (Cardoso et al., 2018; Yampolsky and Yampolsky, 1922). A monoecious plant carries separate male and female flowers on the same plant. In a dioecious species, each individual plant is either male or female. A plant's sexual system shapes how it reproduces. That in turn affects the genes of a plant population and the direction in which it evolves (Barrett, 1992; Fox, 1985; Sabath et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020a). So sexual systems matter for how plant communities and ecosystems are built and how they are kept going (Chen and Li, 2008; Ibarra‐Manríquez and Oyama, 1992). They reflect how vegetation responds to changes in the environment. Across whole regions, they also help steer how forest ecosystems change over long stretches of time (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Charlesworth, 2006; Campbell and Kessler, 2013).

Earlier studies have found strong changes in plant diversity and in the mix of species as latitude changes. Latitude means distance north or south of the equator. These studies also found large differences between world regions such as East Asia and North America (Boufford and Spongberg, 1983; Wang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2017). Most of this work, though, looked at how many species there are, how many different plant groups there are, or at general plant features. Much less attention has gone to how reproductive traits vary across whole plant communities. Among these traits, sexual systems play a basic role in how plants reproduce, how their populations grow and shrink, and how they evolve. Yet we still understand little about how woody plant sexual systems vary across large geographic areas, especially in forests that stretch from the tropics through the subtropics to temperate regions. This gap limits what we know about how reproductive strategies change as the climate changes from place to place, and how they respond to environmental change.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We mapped how common each woody plant sexual system is in 30 forest communities spread across different regions and latitudes. We also compared how non-living factors, such as climate and landscape shape, affect how common each system is. Our results showed that the share of monoecious and dioecious plants changed as latitude changed. Trees and shrubs differed clearly in how common their sexual systems are and in what drives them. These findings shed light on how the sexual systems in forest communities relate to their environment from the equator northward.

Taken together, our study does more than reveal large-scale geographic patterns in the sexual systems of woody plants. It also highlights their use as practical ecological indicators: signs in nature that can help us assess and predict changes in ecosystems caused by climate. Adding sexual systems to long-term forest monitoring programs may greatly improve our ability to detect, understand and reduce the effects of climate change on the variety of life.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent evidence suggests that where different sexual systems turn up depends on many biological and environmental factors. These include a plant's life form (for example, tree or herb), its other reproductive traits, the climate, and the plant's developmental history (Chazdon et al., 2003; Queenborough et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020b). Scientists often study patterns along a latitudinal gradient, moving from the equator toward the poles, to look for large-scale ecological patterns. This works because conditions such as temperature and rainfall change steadily with latitude. Latitude itself, though, does not act on plants directly. It is better thought of as a stand-in on the map for several environmental changes that happen together.

Climate may affect how plants develop their reproductive parts, when they flower, and how they share out their resources. In this way, it may affect which sexual systems appear and where they are found (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Gougherty and Gougherty, 2018; Inouye et al., 2019). Stresses such as drought and very hot or very cold temperatures may also change how plants express their sex and how much they invest in reproduction. They can do this by changing how well plants function and how plants interact with other living things (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016). For example, the environment may change how costly or useful it is for a plant to act as a male or as a female. It may change how well flowers get pollinated. It may also change how a plant splits its resources between growing and reproducing. In the end, these processes can shape which sexual systems appear in a plant community and whether they last there.

So the way plant sexual systems vary from place to place may reflect both broad patterns with latitude and the environmental changes that come with latitude.

Different environmental gradients reflect how varied habitats are and how many resources, such as water and warmth, are available. Because latitude brings together many climate and ecological factors, it gives us a useful way to study large-scale patterns in plant traits across the map. Earlier studies have shown that traits linked to how plants reproduce change in a steady, orderly way as environmental conditions change (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). Still, we largely do not know whether the sexual systems of woody plants follow the same geographic patterns in forests across tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. Answering this question will help us understand how reproductive strategies respond to changes in the environment across large areas.

The link between a plant's sexual system and its growth type (for example, tree, shrub or herb) has received the most attention (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier studies have confirmed that traits tied to sexual systems follow environmental gradients. These traits include a plant's way of life, how long ago its evolutionary line arose, and seed quality (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). So sexual systems, which are closely tied to these traits, may also follow some regular pattern as environmental resources change.

Vamosi et al. (2003) studied 491 genera of flowering plants. (A genus is a group of closely related species.) They found that dioecious plants are more closely linked to woody life forms, especially trees, than monoecious plants are. This link has also been confirmed by studies comparing temperate forests in Sri Lanka and in our own country (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). Wang et al. (2020a) studied 19,780 species of flowering plants in China. They found that the numbers of species with each sexual system differed between woody and non-woody (herbaceous) plants. They also found that the importance of different drivers varied between growth forms. The main drivers were climate, how long ago a group arose in evolution, and how tall the plants grow when mature.

Woody plants usually grow taller, live longer and put more into reproduction than herbaceous plants. This makes them more likely to build up genetic changes over time. Differences in how fast groups evolve may therefore help explain why growth forms differ in how the range of climates they can live in changes over evolution (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014). Even within woody plants, trees and shrubs differ a great deal. They differ in how tall they grow, how long they live, how they gather resources and how much they put into reproduction. Because of these differences, the mix of sexual systems among trees and among shrubs may respond differently to changes in the environment. Exploring where the sexual systems of trees and shrubs are found, and what drives these patterns, will therefore help us understand large-scale patterns in how plants reproduce.

In this study, we used data on the sexual systems of 3,595 species of woody plants from 30 forest communities. We explored the large-scale trends in woody plant sexual systems from the equator northward, and the main environmental factors driving them. Climate and environment vary widely from low latitudes to high latitudes. The 30 forest communities we chose range from wet to dry climates, and from high, flat plateaus to low plains. They run from cold temperate zones in the north, where the seasons set the temperature, to tropical climates and landscapes in the south. This lets us assess geographic patterns in vegetation systems across a wide range of environmental conditions. Overall, we asked three questions: (1) How do plant sexual systems change with latitude across the 30 forest communities? (2) How do the different sexual systems respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in the variety of their sexual systems as latitude changes, and which environmental factors are most closely linked to these patterns?
parts.methods:
2.

What we studied and how

2.1.

Where we studied

For about thirty years, a worldwide research network called the Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO; https://forestgeo.si.edu/what-forestgeo) has gathered long-term information over large areas of tropical, subtropical and temperate forests (Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio; http://www.cfbiodiv.org) has added to this effort, which grew out of an earlier network known as CTFS. CForBio set up large mapped plots at many latitudes, running from temperate through subtropical to tropical forests.

We took 20 plots from ForestGEO and 10 plots from CForBio. The two sets of data are separate, and no plot appears in both. Every plot is one of the large forest plots tracked over many years, and each covers at least 20 hectares. (One hectare is a square 100 meters on each side, a little bigger than a soccer field.) We focused on forests in the Northern Hemisphere, because in the Southern Hemisphere there were few similar long-term plots that also had full information on sexual systems.

Using these 30 forest communities from the two networks, we compared the mix of sexual systems among woody plants as we moved from the equator northward (Figure 1a). The plots lie between 0.2918° N and 61.3000° N, and they sit between 56 and 1,902 meters above sea level. The number of species in a plot ranges from 11 to 408. The plots include some of the richest forests on Earth, such as Xishuangbanna in southwest China (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). These large differences in climate and geography affect how the sexual systems of the plants in each plot change.

In every plot, scientists had counted each tree and measured its trunk if the trunk was at least 1 cm across at breast height (a standard height of about 1.3 meters above the ground, known as DBH, or diameter at breast height). We looked only at trees and shrubs, and left out other plant forms such as climbing vines (lianas) and palms.

Figure 1

Where the 30 forest plots are. The plots range in size from 20 hectares (Xishuangbanna) to 120 hectares (Mpala). They range in latitude from 0.2918° N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3° N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and cover forests in Asia, Europe and North America (a). The number of species with each sexual system in different climate zones (b). A comparison of which species grow in each of the thirty communities, using a method called NMDS, explained in Section 2.3 (c).

2.2.

Information on sexual systems and the environment

We gathered information on 3,595 species from the 30 permanent plots. Different teams recorded these plants in different places and years, so a species' name can be written wrongly or in different ways. To remove such mistakes, we checked the names of every species in every community against two reference works: the Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae (1959–2004), a detailed record of China's plants, and eFloras (http://efloras.org/). When different sources gave a species different sexual systems, we checked it again and again and corrected it.

In some species, the sexual system can change with local conditions, both living and non-living, such as the climate or how many pollinating animals are around (Barrett and Harder, 2017; Schoen, 1982). We left these species out of our analysis. We then sorted the rest by growth form into two types: trees and shrubs.

We took each species' sexual system from the Flora of China (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2, accessed in May 2020), from eFloras, and from a database called Tree of Sex (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we placed each species in one of three groups. Hermaphroditic species have flowers that contain both working male parts (stamens, which make pollen) and working female parts (pistils, which become seeds and fruit) in the same flower. Dioecious species have flowers of only one sex, with female and male flowers on different plants. We also counted in this group mixed forms where some plants carry flowers with both sexes (called androdioecy, gynodioecy and trioecy). Monoecious species have flowers of only one sex, with male and female flowers on the same plant. This group likewise includes mixed forms where one plant also carries flowers with both sexes (called andromonoecy, gynomonoecy and trimonoecy).

For each plot, we also used its longitude and latitude and information on the shape of the land. For the land, we used the average slope (in degrees), the average elevation (in meters), and the highest and lowest elevations (in meters). For climate, we used the average yearly rainfall (in millimeters), the rainfall in the wettest month and in the driest month (in millimeters per month), the average yearly temperature (in °C), and the average temperatures of the warmest and coldest months (in °C). Several of these appear in our figures under short labels: average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average elevation (ME) and average slope (MS).

The longitude, latitude and land information came from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and the Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network. Some plots had no land information from these sources. For those, we took it from maps showing the land's heights and slopes that belong to the monitoring network, and we worked out the values using the methods of Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004). The climate information came from ForestGEO or from published studies (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

We described the sexual systems in each forest plot in two ways that complement each other. First, we worked out what share of the plot's species was monoecious, dioecious or hermaphroditic. This showed how the makeup of sexual systems in a community changes with latitude (Figure 1). Second, we counted the number of species in each group, which scientists call species richness. We used these counts to test how the variety of sexual systems relates to the environment: latitude, climate and the shape of the land (Figure 2).

Figure 2

How the number of woody plant species with each sexual system relates to different conditions in the 30 plots. We used a linear model that takes location into account. In it, the number of species with a given sexual system is the quantity being explained, while climate, land shape and latitude are the factors doing the explaining. The model also allows the leftover errors to be linked between plots, since plots close together tend to be alike. The three rows, from right to left, show all species, tree species and shrubs. The five columns, from top to bottom, show latitude, average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average elevation (ME) and average slope (MS).

2.3.

How we analyzed the data

We chose five environmental factors for our analyses: latitude, average yearly temperature, average yearly rainfall, average elevation and average slope. We chose them because earlier studies have shown that climate, especially temperature and rainfall, along with how varied the land is, strongly shapes plants' reproductive traits and which species live together.

For each of the 30 forest communities, we worked out the share of species with each sexual system, based on the species recorded there. To show how this mix differed between climate zones, we drew alluvial diagrams, charts where colored bands flow between categories and their widths show how large each group is. We made them with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We also used graphs to show how the number of species differed among the sexual-system groups.

To compare which species grow in each community, we used a method called non-metric multidimensional scaling, or NMDS (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). NMDS draws each community as a point on a map. Communities with similar mixes of species end up close together, and very different ones end up far apart. A number called "stress" tells us how well this map fits the real data and whether the arrangement is sensible. In our study, NMDS arranged the 30 plots according to how many plants of each woody species they contained. We then drew circles around plots from the same climate zone to show how the makeup of forest communities differed between zones.

We used linear regression to explore how latitude and the environment affect the sexual systems of woody plants. The quantities we tried to explain were the numbers of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. The explaining factors were latitude, average yearly temperature, average yearly rainfall, average elevation and average slope. We used the plain count of species in each group. We did not divide it by the total number of species in the plot.

When explaining factors move together closely, for example when colder places are also higher up, it becomes hard to tell their effects apart. To check for this problem, we calculated a measure called the variance inflation factor, or VIF, for each factor (Supplementary Table 1). All the values were below 10, which means this overlap was at an acceptable level. We used a score called the adjusted R² to show how much of the change in species from place to place the environmental factors could explain (Tang et al., 2012). Adding many explaining factors can make a model look better than it really is. To avoid this, we compared the models using a score, an information criterion, that rewards a close fit but penalizes extra factors. With it, we chose the best environmental model and the best model that takes location into account.

We also used redundancy analysis (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). This method combines regression with another technique, principal component analysis, that boils many measurements down to a few main patterns. Here, the data to be explained were the numbers of plants in the three sexual-system groups. The explaining data were the environmental factors: longitude and latitude, the four land measures (average slope, average elevation, highest elevation and lowest elevation) and the six climate measures (average yearly rainfall, rainfall in the wettest and driest months, average yearly temperature, and the average temperatures of the warmest and coldest months). We used a function called "envfit" to test how environmental factors affect the spread of sexual systems among woody plant communities. It shuffles the data at random 999 times to see how often a link as strong as the real one appears by chance.

To compare more closely how non-living factors (latitude, land shape and climate) affect the pattern of sexual systems, we built a structural equation model (Grace, 2006). This is a statistical method based on regression. In it, we assumed that the non-living factors taken together directly affect the pattern of sexual systems. We also assumed that latitude, average yearly temperature, rainfall in the wettest month, the average temperature of the warmest month and average slope each affect the pattern, either directly or through other factors. The full model has two parts. An inner part links hidden quantities that cannot be measured directly. An outer part links those hidden quantities to the things we actually measured. In our study, the hidden quantity is the number of species with each sexual system, and the measured quantities are the environmental factors.

The model also allowed the numbers of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species to vary together. Together, these three groups describe the sexual-system makeup of a community, so they do not vary independently of one another. In our diagrams, arrows pointing both ways show that two quantities vary together, not that one causes the other.

We ran all the analyses in the statistics program R, version 4.0.3 (R Core Development Team). We drew the alluvial diagrams with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We ran NMDS and redundancy analysis with the "vegan" package (Oksanen et al., 2010), and structural equation modeling with the "lavaan" package (Rosseel et al., 2012).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

A pattern in sexual systems from the tropics northward

We looked at how the sexual systems of woody plants are spread across 30 forest plots in tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. The share of monoecious species in a plot generally rose as we moved north, away from the equator. Hermaphroditic species showed the opposite trend. These are species whose flowers each hold both male and female parts in the same flower. The share of dioecious species stayed fairly steady from south to north (Figure 1b). Together, these trends suggest that the mix of sexual systems in a forest changes in a regular way from one climate zone to another.

We also asked how different the 30 forest communities were in the species they contained. To do this, we used a method called non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS). It places the communities on a kind of map so that forests with similar species sit close together and very different forests sit far apart. We based the map on a common measure of how different two species lists are, called Bray–Curtis dissimilarity. A number called "stress" shows how well the map fits the real differences, and lower is better. The stress here was 0.031. The map showed that the species found in the 30 communities differed significantly (Figure 1c).

Figure 1 has three panels. Panel a shows where the 30 plots are. They run from 0.29°N at Mpala, Republic of the Congo, to 61.3°N at Scotty Creek, Canada, and range in size from 20 ha to 120 ha. Panel b shows what share of the species in each climate zone are monoecious, dioecious or hermaphroditic. Panel c shows the NMDS map of how the forest communities differ in their species. We included only plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there were too few comparable long-term forest plots with full information on sexual systems.

3.2.

How non-living factors relate to the number of species with each sexual system

We used linear regression to see how the number of species with each sexual system, called species richness, changed with latitude and with mean annual temperature (MAT, the average temperature over a whole year). To judge how close each link was, we used a number called adjusted R². It shows what share of the ups and downs in species richness a factor can account for, from 0 (none) to 1 (all). It is "adjusted" to make fair comparisons between models. Hermaphroditic species showed the closest links with latitude and temperature. Their adjusted R² was 0.413 for all woody plants together, 0.511 for trees and 0.412 for shrubs. Links were looser for monoecious species (0.181 for all woody plants, 0.412 for trees and 0.100 for shrubs). Dioecious species fell in between (0.353 for all woody plants, 0.419 for trees and 0.310 for shrubs) (Figure 2).

For monoecious and dioecious species, richness was more closely tied to temperature than to latitude. With temperature, the adjusted R² was 0.421 for monoecious species (P < 0.001) and 0.544 for dioecious species (P < 0.005). With latitude, it was only 0.181 for monoecious species (P < 0.001) and 0.343 for dioecious species (P < 0.001). The P value tells us whether a link is statistically significant. We call a result statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. For P < 0.05, that means less than 5% of the time. Smaller P values mean such a pattern would be even rarer by chance.

For all three sexual systems, the number of species fell significantly as latitude increased and rose significantly as mean annual temperature increased (Figure 2). When we looked at trees and shrubs separately, the number of species with each sexual system was most closely linked to latitude and temperature. Mean annual precipitation (MAP, the total rain and snow in a year) came next. Links with slope and mean elevation (ME, the average height of the land above sea level) were the weakest. Overall, the number of species was much less closely tied to landscape shape (mean elevation and mean slope) than to climate. Even so, we did find some significant links for certain sexual systems and for trees or shrubs (Figures 2d, e).

Next, we used redundancy analysis to see how well the environment explains which sexual systems make up each community. The environmental factors together explained 7.57% of the differences among communities for monoecious plants, 8.45% for dioecious plants and 7.37% for hermaphroditic plants. In each case, that is the share of all the variation among communities that the environment could account for. For all three sexual systems, longitude (position east or west) and mean annual temperature were the most important factors. Precipitation of the wettest month (PWM, the rain and snow that falls in the year's wettest month) was also important for all three. For trees, climate factors mattered most. For shrubs, longitude mattered most (Figure 3).

Figure 3

Results of the redundancy analysis for monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic communities, shown separately for different plant life forms (trees and shrubs). The ellipses show 95% confidence intervals, the zone where we expect most of each group's points to fall. Stars mark significant links between communities and environmental factors: "***" is the strongest (P < 0.001), "**" is strong (P < 0.01) and "*" is significant (P < 0.05). Abbreviations: MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, precipitation of the wettest month; PDM, precipitation of the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

3.3.

How climate affects the number of species with each sexual system

We then built a structural equation model. It links climate, landscape shape and location to the number of species with each sexual system. Each arrow in the model has a "path coefficient." This number shows how strongly one factor is tied to another, on a shared scale so that different arrows can be compared. The larger it is, the stronger the link. In our model, the climate factors were positively linked to the number of species in all three sexual systems. These factors were mean annual temperature, the mean temperature of the warmest month (MTWM) and precipitation of the wettest month. The path coefficients from climate were 0.88 for monoecious plants, 0.70 for dioecious plants and 0.77 for hermaphroditic plants. All three were larger than the links from landscape shape and location (Figure 4).

Trees and shrubs differed. The path coefficient from climate to dioecious trees (0.88) was lower than that for shrubs (0.96). Meanwhile, the coefficients for dioecious shrubs (0.81) and hermaphroditic shrubs (0.90) were higher than those for trees (0.75 and 0.57) (Figure 4). The model shows that each sexual-system group responds to the environment in its own way. The monoecious group had a more significant relationship with environmental factors than the dioecious group did.

Figure 4

This path diagram shows how climate, landscape shape and location connect to the number of species with each sexual system. The climate factors are temperature (MAT) and precipitation (MTWM and PWM). Landscape shape is mean slope (MS), and location is latitude. The number next to each arrow is its path coefficient on a shared scale. Red numbers show negative links and blue numbers show positive links. Thicker arrows show stronger links. "***" marks paths with P < 0.001, "**" marks paths with P < 0.01 and "*" marks paths with P < 0.05.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

We found a clear trend in how many species belonged to each sexual system in forest communities at different latitudes and in different regions. These large-scale patterns differed from one sexual system to another, and they also differed between trees and shrubs. Climate explained a large part of these differences.

4.1.

How the variety of sexual systems changes from the equator northward

In this study, we compared the shares of different sexual systems in forests in the tropics, the subtropics and the temperate zone, moving from the equator northward. The first group we looked at was hermaphroditic species, whose flowers each hold both male and female parts. In both East Asia and North America, their share did not rise or fall in a statistically significant way with latitude. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no trend at all, a pattern this strong would rarely turn up by chance alone. "Not significant" means we could not show a trend. It does not prove that none exists.

The share of dioecious species, on the other hand, went up as latitude went down, that is, closer to the equator. Monoecious and dioecious species followed opposite trends, and this contrast creates strong geographic differences from the equator northward (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006). Overall, our results show that the share of monoecious species rises with latitude, while the share of dioecious species falls with latitude. To some extent, this suggests that the shares of monoecious and dioecious species may be closely tied to region, and especially to latitude. The share of hermaphroditic plants, however, showed no clear pattern with latitude (Chen and Li, 2008).

Early studies found more dioecious species than monoecious species in the tropics, close to the equator (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also backed up our findings: many tropical tree species that grow at low density include a higher share of dioecious species. More recently, however, Wang et al. (2021) used nearly 70,000 species of flowering plants to study how sexual systems are spread across the whole globe. They confirmed that both dioecious and monoecious species appear more often at high latitudes, far from the equator. Other studies have found that dioecious species are more common at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere. Studies in the North and in Siberia found that the share of dioecious species rises with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017). The pattern we see today in where flowering plants with different sexual systems grow is due to dioecious and monoecious plants being able to handle a wider range of conditions and to spread their seeds more widely. Our findings may also reflect the fact that we used data from the first full species counts in these large plots, and so they agree with earlier studies by others (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

4.2.

How climate affects the number of species in each sexual system

Scientists who study how plants reproduce have found that sexual systems, and the ways of mating they lead to, are very sensitive to changes in climate and in geographic surroundings (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). A correlation is a link in which two things tend to change together. In our results, hermaphroditic plants had a stronger correlation with latitude and with mean annual temperature (MAT, the average temperature over a year) than monoecious and dioecious plants did. Across the three sexual systems, both trees and shrubs showed their strongest links with latitude and mean annual temperature (Figure 2).

Climate, meaning temperature and rainfall, can also affect how a plant's sexual system shows itself. It does this by changing how the plant's body works and how it lives in its surroundings, and by controlling how well it reproduces while it is flowering (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). We tested many possible models, or explanations built from different sets of environmental conditions. The models that best explained the share of each of the three sexual systems included measures of temperature and rainfall. This was true for all species together, for trees alone and for shrubs alone (Figure 4). Other conditions may also affect how the shares of sexual systems vary from place to place. These include the shape of the land, mean annual precipitation (MAP, total yearly rainfall), precipitation of the driest month (PDM) and mean temperature of the coldest month (MTCM), for all species, trees and shrubs respectively. But their effects were weaker than those of mean annual temperature and precipitation of the wettest month (PWM).

These findings suggest that climate should be the main driver of which sexual systems a forest contains and how varied they are. This may be because of ongoing climate change, such as less rainfall and warmer winters, and because of changes in the timing of plant life events, such as earlier flowering (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). Male and female plants need different amounts of resources. These differences then affect how populations are made up, which sexual systems are found in a place, and even how the variety of sexual systems is spread across the map (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Our other findings agree with studies of what decides which species live in forest communities, at both small and large scales (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study looked at how environmental stress affects the balance of males and females in flowering plants. It found a statistically significant correlation between the shares of monoecious and dioecious species and climate, meaning temperature and rainfall (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). In short, our results confirm recent findings that temperature and rainfall are major drivers of where sexual systems are found in communities of woody plants. They also suggest that the effects of location itself should not be ignored when we try to explain what shapes the mix of sexual systems in a forest.

Our results therefore suggest that sexual systems are not just traits shaped by evolution. They are also working ecological indicators, signs in nature that tie together how plants reproduce and the conditions they live in. Because sexual systems are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, tracking shifts in how common monoecious and dioecious species are could give valuable clues about how forest communities are responding to ongoing climate change. This points to plant sexual systems as a new, trait-based way to track the variety of life as the world warms.

We should also note how we counted. We used the actual number of species in each sexual system, rather than adjusting it for the total number of species in each plot. Because of this, some of the geographic patterns we saw may partly reflect differences in how many species each plot holds overall, and not only changes in the mix of sexual systems. Future studies that adjust for the total number of species, or that measure how abundant each species is, may help separate these effects.

4.3.

How non-living factors affect sexual systems in trees and in shrubs

Our structural equation model showed that climate and land shape had stronger statistically significant links with the three sexual systems in trees than in shrubs (Figure 4). This agrees with earlier large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Trees generally live longer and grow bigger. Their parts above the ground stay exposed to the weather for long periods, which may make them more sensitive to long-term changes in their surroundings (Wang et al., 2020a). So climate has a stronger effect on where trees grow than on where shrubs grow (Currie and Paquin, 1987). These results suggest that climate may affect the geographic patterns of sexual systems differently in trees and shrubs partly because the two growth forms have different ways of gathering and using resources such as water, light and nutrients.

One limitation of this study is that we did not directly include in our analyses how closely related the species are to one another, that is, their places on the plant family tree. Sexual systems often stay the same across a branch of the family tree, so closely related species may share similar ways of reproducing because they share ancestors. This means some of the geographic patterns we saw may partly reflect which plant families happen to live in each forest, or the history of how plants spread across the land, rather than only the environment sorting which species can live where. Future studies that include family-tree information would help separate how much evolutionary history and how much the environment each contribute to the large-scale differences in the sexual systems of woody plants.

4.4.

How sexual systems could help us keep watch on forests

Our findings suggest that the mix of sexual systems in a forest, especially the shares of dioecious and monoecious species, may be a useful trait-based sign of environmental conditions. Tracking changes in this mix may add useful information to long-term forest monitoring networks such as ForestGEO and CForBio. Because where each sexual system is found was significantly linked with climate, tracking changes in the mix of sexual systems may add information on how forest communities respond to differences in their surroundings. However, this study compares places with different climates at one point in time, rather than following the same places over time. It therefore does not directly test how well sexual systems work as signs of ongoing climate change.

Traditional methods such as remote sensing, which studies forests from satellites or aircraft, often focus on how green the treetops are or how much plant material there is. Compared with these, the mix of sexual systems may give extra insight into how plants reproduce and how forest communities come together. Still, tracking sexual systems over large areas needs long-term fieldwork and experts who can identify species, which may limit its use when a quick check is needed. Future studies that combine sexual-system tracking with remote sensing and databases of plant traits may offer a fuller way to follow how the variety of life responds to environmental change.

parts.title: How the Sexual Systems of Woody Plants Change with Latitude in Northern Hemisphere Forests, and What Drives the Pattern
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

Every plant has a "sexual system": a way its male and female parts are arranged. This arrangement is a key trait that shapes how communities of woody plants (trees and shrubs) live and evolve. Yet we still do not understand well how it varies from warmer to cooler climates.

Methods

We gathered information on 3,595 woody species from 30 forest dynamics plots. These are large forest areas where every tree is tracked over many years. The plots span tropical, subtropical, and temperate zones across the Northern Hemisphere. We looked for large-scale patterns with three statistical tools: linear regression, redundancy analysis, and structural equation modeling.

Results

As we moved to higher latitudes (farther from the equator), the share of monoecious species went up and the share of dioecious species went down. Monoecious plants carry separate male and female flowers on the same individual. Dioecious plants have male and female flowers on different individuals. Climate was the main driver of these patterns, especially temperature and rainfall. The links between climate and sexual systems were stronger in trees than in shrubs.

Discussion

Our results show that where woody plants grow is closely tied to which sexual systems they have, and that climate gradients are part of the story. Monoecious and dioecious species changed in a consistent way along these gradients. This shows that sexual systems matter ecologically. It also suggests they may give us useful trait-based information about how forest communities respond to environmental change. More long-term studies are needed to find out how useful they could be for monitoring forests as the climate changes.

Keywords: climate change, ecological indicator, latitudinal gradient, sexual systems, woody plants
parts.introduction_first: One of the biggest patterns in nature is that the number of species drops as you travel from the equator toward the poles. We can see this pattern in forests across different climate zones. Flowers are the sexual organs of a plant, so they are part of how it reproduces. Plants arrange their male and female parts in different ways, which we call sexual systems. Some plants are monoecious or dioecious, and some have more complex arrangements. A plant's sexual system affects how it reproduces. That in turn affects the genetic makeup of its populations and the direction their evolution takes. For this reason, sexual systems help build and sustain plant communities and whole ecosystems. They show how vegetation responds to environmental change, and they also shape how forest ecosystems evolve across a region. Earlier studies found strong latitudinal gradients in plant diversity and in which species make up a community. These gradients differ between regions such as East Asia and North America. Most of that work, however, looked at the number of species, how many kinds of plants there are, or other functional traits. Very little looked at how reproductive traits vary within whole communities. Sexual systems are a basic part of how plants reproduce, how populations change, and how species evolve. Even so, we still know little about their large-scale geographic patterns in woody plants, especially across forests that stretch from tropical to subtropical to temperate regions. This gap means we do not yet understand how reproductive strategies change along climate gradients or respond to environmental change.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We mapped how often each woody plant sexual system occurs along the latitudes of 30 forest communities in different regions. We also compared how non-living environmental factors, such as climate and terrain, affect those frequencies. We found that the frequencies of monoecious and dioecious plants change along the latitude gradient. We also found significant differences between trees and shrubs, both in how common each sexual system is and in what shapes it. These findings show how the sexual systems of forest communities are related to environmental factors along latitude gradients. Taken together, our study reveals large-scale geographic patterns in woody plant sexual systems. It also shows that sexual systems can serve as practical ecological indicators, helping us assess and predict ecosystem changes driven by climate. If we build sexual system changes into long-term forest monitoring, we may significantly improve our ability to detect and interpret the effects of climate change on biodiversity, and to reduce them.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent evidence suggests that many things shape how sexual systems vary from place to place. These include a plant's life form (for example, tree or shrub), its reproductive traits, the climate, and its developmental history (Chazdon et al., 2003; Queenborough et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020b).

Scientists often use latitude gradients to study large-scale patterns in nature, because latitude goes hand in hand with steady changes in climate, such as temperature and rainfall. But latitude is not itself a direct cause of anything. It stands in for several environmental gradients that change together as you move away from the equator.

Climate can act directly on how plants develop their reproductive parts, when they flower, and how they divide their resources. In this way it can affect which sexual systems occur and where (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Gougherty and Gougherty, 2018; Inouye et al., 2019). Stresses such as drought and extreme temperatures can also change which sex a plant expresses and how much energy it puts into reproduction. They do this by affecting how well plants function and how they interact with one another (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016).

For example, the environment may change the relative costs and benefits of being male or female. It may change how successfully flowers are pollinated, or how a plant splits its resources between growing and reproducing. Over time, these processes can shape which sexual systems appear and last in a plant community.

So geographic variation in sexual systems may reflect two things: the broad patterns along latitude, and the environmental gradients that lie behind them.

Different environmental gradients reflect differences in how varied habitats are and how many resources are available. Because latitude bundles together many climate and ecological factors, it is a useful frame for studying large-scale geographic patterns in plant traits. Earlier studies have shown that traits tied to how plants reproduce change in regular ways along environmental gradients (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). Still, we know very little about whether the sexual systems of woody plants follow consistent geographic patterns across forests that run from tropical through subtropical to temperate regions. Answering this would help us understand how reproductive strategies respond to environmental change across wide areas.

The link between sexual system and growth type (such as tree, shrub, or herb) has received the most attention (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier work has confirmed that traits related to sexual system, such as life style, how old a plant group is in evolutionary terms, and seed quality, are spread out along environmental gradients (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). So the closely related sexual system may also show a spatial pattern along gradients of environmental resources.

Vamosi et al. (2003) studied 491 angiosperm genera (angiosperms are flowering plants). They found that dioecious plants are linked more strongly with woody life forms, especially trees, than monoecious plants are. Studies of temperate forests in Sri Lanka and in our own country have confirmed this link (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). Wang et al. (2020a) studied 19,780 angiosperms in China. They found that woody and herbaceous (non-woody) species differ in how many of each sexual system they have. They also found that the importance of different drivers, particularly climate, evolutionary age, and the height of a mature plant, varied among growth forms.

Woody plants generally have taller canopies, longer lives, and put more into reproduction than herbaceous plants. This makes them more likely to build up genetic changes over time. Differences in how fast they evolve may therefore help explain why growth forms differ in how their climate niche (the range of climates they live in) evolves (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014).

Even among woody plants, trees and shrubs differ a great deal in canopy height, lifespan, how they gather resources, and how they spend energy on reproduction. These differences may lead their sexual-system makeup to respond differently to environmental gradients. So studying the geographic spread of sexual systems in trees and in shrubs, and what drives it, will help us understand large-scale geographic patterns in plant reproductive strategies.

Here we used data on the sexual systems of 3,595 woody plant species in 30 forest communities. We explored the large-scale trend in woody plant sexual systems along the latitude gradient, and the main environmental factors behind it. Climates and environments vary a lot from low latitudes to high latitudes. The 30 forests we chose range from humid to dry climates and from plateau to plain landscapes. They also range from cold temperate zones in the north, defined by seasonal temperatures, to tropical climates and landscapes in the south. This lets us look at geographic patterns in sexual systems across a wide range of environments.

We asked three questions. (1) What are the latitude patterns of sexual systems across the 30 forest communities? (2) How does the spread of different sexual systems respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in sexual-system diversity along latitude gradients, and which environmental factors are mainly linked to these patterns?
parts.methods:
2. What we used and how we did the study

2.1. Where the study took place

For the past three decades, the Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO) has collected long-term, large-scale data on tropical, subtropical and temperate forests (https://forestgeo.si.edu/what-forestgeo; Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio; http://www.cfbiodiv.org) has added to this network. It has set up large mapped plots along a latitude gradient that runs through temperate, subtropical and tropical forests. We took twenty plots from ForestGEO and ten from CForBio. The two datasets are independent, and no plot appears in both. Every plot is a large forest dynamics plot of 20 hectares or more.

We focused on forest plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there are few comparable long-term plots with complete information on sexual systems. In this study, we compare the sexual-system makeup of woody plants along a latitude gradient in 30 forest communities from these two networks (Figure 1a). The plots lie between 0.2918° N and 61.3000° N, at altitudes of 56 to 1902 meters. The number of species per plot ranges from 11 to 408. The set includes some of the most species-rich forests in the world, such as Xishuangbanna (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). We expect these differences in climate and geography to affect how the sexual systems of forest plants vary from plot to plot.

In every plot, the trees were counted and their trunks measured down to a diameter of 1 cm or more at breast height. We studied only trees and shrubs. We left out other growth forms, namely lianas (climbing vines) and palms.

Figure 1

Where the 30 forest plots are located. Plots range in size from 20 ha (Xishuangbanna) to 120 ha (Mpala). They range in latitude from 0.2918° N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3° N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and they cover forests in Asia, Europe and North America (a). Panel b shows the number of species with each sexual system in different climate zones. Panel c shows an NMDS analysis (a way of drawing how similar the plots' species are) of the species makeup of the thirty communities.

2.2. Data on sexual systems and the environment

We collected information on 3595 species from the 30 permanent monitoring plots. Species lists can contain mistakes because they were made at different times, in different places and by different people. To remove these, we checked the species names in every community against the Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae (1959–2004) and eFloras (http://efloras.org/). Where different sources gave conflicting sexual systems for a species, we checked again and corrected the record. The sexual system of some species can change with local living and non-living conditions, such as climate or the number of pollinators (Barrett and Harder, 2017; Schoen, 1982). We left these species out of the analysis. We also sorted the plants by growth form into two types: trees and shrubs.

We took the sexual systems of these woody plants from the Flora of China (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2, accessed in May 2020), eFloras and the Tree of Sex database (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we sorted them into three groups. Hermaphroditic species have both working male parts (stamens) and female parts (pistils) in the same flower. Dioecious species have single-sex flowers, with female and male flowers on different individuals. This group includes androdioecy, gynodioecy and trioecy. Monoecious species also have single-sex flowers, but male and female flowers grow on the same individual. This group includes andromonoecy, gynomonoecy and trimonoecy.

For each plot, we used its longitude and latitude, along with measures of the terrain and the climate. The terrain measures were mean slope (MS, in degrees), mean elevation (ME, in meters), highest elevation (HA, in meters) and lowest elevation (LE, in meters). The climate measures were mean annual precipitation (MAP, in mm), precipitation of the wettest month (PWM, mm per month), precipitation of the driest month (PDM, mm per month), mean annual temperature (MAT, °C), and the mean temperature of the warmest month (MTWM, °C) and of the coldest month (MTCM, °C).

We took latitude, longitude and terrain data from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and from the Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network. Where these institutions gave no terrain data for a plot, we worked it out from the network's topographic maps. We used the methods of Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004) for this. The climate data came from ForestGEO or from published papers (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

For each plot, we described the sexual systems in two complementary ways. First, we calculated the share of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. This shows how the sexual-system makeup of the community changes along the latitude gradient (Figure 1). Second, we counted the species in each sexual-system group, which we call species richness. We used these counts to test how the number of species with each sexual system relates to environmental variables, including latitude, climate and terrain (Figure 2).

Figure 2

How the number of species with each sexual system relates to different variables in the 30 plots. We used a spatial linear model. The number of species with a given sexual system was the outcome. Climate variables, terrain variables and latitude were the several factors that might explain it. The model also allowed for errors that carry over between nearby plots (autoregressive errors). The three rows, from right to left, show all species, tree species and shrub species. The five columns, from top to bottom, show latitude, mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean elevation (ME) and mean slope (MS).

2.3. How we analyzed the data

We chose five environmental variables for the analyses: latitude, MAT, MAP, ME and MS. Earlier studies have shown that climate, especially temperature and rainfall, and the variety of terrain are major drivers of plant reproductive traits and of which species live together.

For each of the 30 forest communities, we worked out the share of woody species in each sexual system from the species recorded there. We drew how sexual systems are spread across climate zones as alluvial diagrams (flow charts whose bands show how groups divide up), using the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We also showed the differences in species numbers among the sexual-system groups in graphs.

We used non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) to compare the communities. NMDS places each community as a point on a map. The distance between two points shows how different their species are (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). A number called the stress coefficient tells us how well the map fits the data and whether the ordering makes sense. We ranked the abundance of woody plants in the 30 plots with NMDS. We then drew circles around the points to show how species makeup differs among forests in different climate zones.

We used linear regression to test how latitude and environmental factors affect the sexual systems of woody plants. Linear regression asks whether a straight-line relationship links one outcome to the factors that might explain it. The outcomes were the number of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. The explanatory factors were latitude, MAT, MAP, ME and MS. We analyzed the actual number of species and did not adjust it for the total number of species in each plot.

We checked whether the explanatory variables overlapped too much with each other, which is called multicollinearity. For this we used the variance inflation factor (VIF; Supplementary Table 1). All VIF values were below 10, which means the overlap was at an acceptable level. We used the adjusted R² to show how much of the variation in species turnover (how much the set of species changes from place to place) the environmental and spatial variables explain (Tang et al., 2012). Adding more variables can make a model look better than it is. To avoid this, we compared the models' information criterion scores, a measure that balances fit against complexity. From these we chose the best environmental model and the best spatial model.

We also used redundancy analysis (RDA). It is a ranking method that combines regression with principal component analysis, a way of boiling many measurements down to a few main directions (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). The responses were the abundances of the three woody-plant sexual systems. The explanatory variables were longitude and latitude, the terrain measures (MS, ME, HA and LE) and the climate measures (MAP, PWM, PDM, MAT, MTWM and MTCM). To study how these factors affect the spread of sexual systems across communities, we used the "envfit" function with 999 permutations. In a permutation test, the data are shuffled 999 times to see what results chance alone would produce.

To compare further how non-living factors (latitude, terrain and climate) affect the spread of sexual systems, we built a structural equation model (SEM). We assumed that the total effect of the non-living factors acts directly on how sexual systems are distributed. We also assumed that latitude, MAT, PWM, MTWM and MS act on it either directly or indirectly. An SEM is a statistical method built on regression (Grace, 2006). A full path model has an internal part, the relationships between hidden (latent) variables, and an external part, the relationships between those hidden variables and what we actually measure. Here the hidden variable is the richness of woody-plant sexual systems, and the measured variables are the environmental factors.

The SEM also included covariances (how much two quantities rise and fall together) among the richness of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. These three groups together describe the sexual-system makeup of a community, so they are not statistically independent of each other. Double-headed arrows in the model show covariance, not cause and effect.

We ran all analyses in R 4.0.3 (R Core Team). We made the alluvial plots with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We ran NMDS and RDA with the "vegan" package (Oksanen et al., 2010), and the SEM with the "lavaan" package (Rosseel et al., 2012).
parts.results:
## 3. Results

### 3.1. How sexual systems change from the tropics to colder regions

We looked at how the sexual systems of woody plants are spread across 30 forest plots. The plots cover tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. As we moved to higher latitudes, the share of monoecious species generally went up, while the share of hermaphroditic species went down. Dioecious species behaved differently: their share stayed fairly steady along the latitude gradient (Figure 1b). Together, these trends suggest that the mix of sexual systems changes in a regular way from one climate zone to another.

Figure 1 shows the details. Panel a is a map of the 30 plots. They run from 0.29°N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3°N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and each plot covers between 20 and 120 hectares. Panel b shows what share of the species in each climate zone are monoecious, dioecious, or hermaphroditic.

Panel c uses a method called NMDS. It draws each forest community as a point on a map, so that communities with similar mixes of species sit close together and very different ones sit far apart. The map showed significant differences in species makeup among the 30 forest communities (Bray–Curtis stress = 0.031). Bray–Curtis is the measure we used for how different two species lists are. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no differences, gaps this large would rarely turn up by chance alone.

We used only plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere there were few comparable long-term forest plots with complete sexual-system information.

### 3.2. How non-living environmental factors shape the number of species in each sexual system

Here we counted the species in each sexual system (the plant's "richness" for that system) and asked how well each environmental factor lines up with those counts. We scored the link with a number called adjusted R², which runs from 0 to 1. A value of 0.413, for example, means the factor accounts for about 41% of the ups and downs in the species counts across plots. Higher numbers mean a closer link.

The number of hermaphroditic species was linked fairly strongly to latitude and to mean annual temperature (MAT). The adjusted R² was 0.413 for all hermaphroditic plants together, 0.511 for trees, and 0.412 for shrubs. Those links were stronger than the ones for monoecious plants (0.181 overall, 0.412 for trees, 0.100 for shrubs) and for dioecious plants (0.353 overall, 0.419 for trees, 0.310 for shrubs) (Figure 2).

For monoecious and dioecious plants, species counts matched temperature better than they matched latitude. With MAT, the adjusted R² was 0.421 for monoecious plants (P < 0.001) and 0.544 for dioecious plants (P < 0.005). With latitude, it was 0.181 for monoecious plants (P < 0.001) and 0.343 for dioecious plants (P < 0.001). All three sexual systems had significantly fewer species at higher latitudes and significantly more species in places with higher MAT (Figure 2).

When we looked at trees and shrubs separately, the species counts for each sexual system were linked most strongly to latitude and MAT. Next came mean annual precipitation (MAP). The weakest links were with mean slope and mean elevation. Topography (mean elevation and mean slope) was generally a weak match for species counts compared with climate. Still, we did find some significant links for particular sexual systems and growth forms (Figures 2d, e).

Next we asked how much the environment explains about the makeup of each group of communities. The environmental variables we measured explained 7.57% of the variation in the makeup of monoecious communities, 8.45% for dioecious communities, and 7.37% for hermaphroditic communities. This came from redundancy analysis (RDA), a method that shows how much of the differences between communities can be matched to a set of environmental factors.

In the RDA, longitude and MAT were the most important factors for all three sexual systems. Precipitation of the wettest month (PWM) was also an important factor for all three. When we split plants into trees and shrubs, the more important factors were climate for trees and longitude for shrubs (Figure 3).

**Figure 3.** Maps of monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic plant communities from redundancy analysis (RDA), shown for each plant life form. The ellipses mark the 95% confidence interval. Stars show how strongly a community is linked to an environmental factor: "***" is the strongest link (P < 0.001), "**" a strong link (P < 0.01), and "*" a link (P < 0.05). Abbreviations: MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, precipitation of the wettest month; PDM, precipitation of the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

### 3.3. How climate affects the number of species in each sexual system

Finally, we used structural equation modeling (SEM). This method draws arrows between factors and gives each arrow a "path coefficient," a number showing how strongly one factor is tied to another. In our SEM, the climate factors (MAT, MTWM, and PWM) were positively linked to the number of species in all three sexual systems. The path coefficients were 0.88 for monoecious, 0.70 for dioecious, and 0.77 for hermaphroditic plants. In each case these were greater than the coefficients for topography and for space (Figure 4).

The results differed between life forms. For dioecious plants, the coefficient for climate was lower in trees (0.88) than in shrubs (0.96). For shrubs, the coefficients for dioecious (0.81) and hermaphroditic (0.90) plants were higher than those for trees (0.75 and 0.57, respectively) (Figure 4).

These SEM results show that the sexual systems respond differently to environmental variables. The link between monoecious plants and the environmental variables was more significant than the link for dioecious plants.

**Figure 4.** A path diagram of how climate (temperature: MAT; precipitation: MTWM and PWM), topography (MS), space (latitude), and the number of species in each sexual system are connected. The number beside each arrow is its standardized path coefficient. Red numbers mean a negative link and blue numbers a positive link. Thicker arrows mean stronger links. Stars show how significant a path is: "***" for P < 0.001, "**" for P < 0.01, and "*" for P < 0.05.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

We found a clear trend with latitude in the number of species of each sexual system in forest communities across different regions. The patterns differed from one sexual system to another, and they differed between trees and shrubs. Climate explained a large share of this variation.

4.1.

Sexual systems change along the latitude gradient

We compared how common each sexual system was in forests in the tropics, the subtropics, and the temperate zones. In East Asia and North America, the share of hermaphrodite species (plants whose flowers have both male and female parts) did not rise or fall in a statistically significant way along the latitude gradient. The share of dioecious species did change: it grew as latitude got lower, toward the equator. Monoecious and dioecious species moved in opposite directions, and that contrast creates strong geographic differences along the whole latitude gradient (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006). Put simply, the share of monoecious species goes up with latitude, while the share of dioecious species goes down. This suggests that the shares of monoecious and dioecious species may be closely linked to region, and especially to latitude. The share of hermaphroditic plants, however, showed no obvious pattern along the latitude gradient (Chen and Li, 2008).

Early studies found more dioecious than monoecious species in tropical regions at low latitudes (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also supported our findings: many tropical tree species that live at low density have a high share of dioecious species. More recently, though, Wang et al. (2021) used nearly 70,000 flowering plant species to map sexual systems across the whole world. They confirmed that both dioecious and monoecious species are more frequent at high latitudes. Other studies have found that dioecious species are more common at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere, and work in the north and in Siberia found that the share of dioecious species increases with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017). We think the sexual-system pattern we see today comes from the wider tolerance of different environments, and the stronger ability to spread, of dioecious and monoecious plants. Our findings may also be related to the data we used. These were the first species census data from these large plots, and our results are consistent with earlier studies by others (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

4.2.

How climate affects the number of species of each sexual system

In plant reproduction research, it is well known that sexual systems, and the mating patterns they set up, react strongly to changes in climate and in the physical environment (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). In our results, hermaphroditic plants were more strongly linked to latitude and to mean annual temperature (MAT) than monoecious or dioecious plants were. Within each of the three sexual systems, both trees and shrubs showed their strongest links with latitude and MAT (Figure 2).

Temperature and rainfall can also shape which sexual system a plant shows. They do this by changing the plant's body and its ecology, and by affecting how well it reproduces while it flowers (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). We used structural equation models, which test how several factors link together to influence an outcome. In the best models, temperature and rainfall measures were always chosen to explain the share of each sexual system, whether we looked at all species, at trees, or at shrubs (Figure 4). Other factors, namely terrain, mean annual precipitation, precipitation in the driest month, and temperature in the coldest month, may also affect how the shares vary from place to place, for all species, trees, and shrubs respectively. But their effects were weaker than those of MAT and the other rainfall measure we used, PWM. These findings suggest that climate should be the main driver of which sexual systems make up a forest and how diverse they are.

Ongoing climate change may play a part here, for example less rain and warmer winters, along with shifts in plant timing such as earlier flowering (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). Plants of different sexes need different amounts of resources, and these differences may in turn affect the structure of populations, the local mix of sexual systems, and even where in the world they are found (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Our other findings agree with studies of what decides which species live together in forests at different scales (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study of how environmental stress affects the sex ratio in flowering plants found a significant link between the ratio of monoecious to dioecious species and climate, meaning temperature and precipitation (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). In short, our results back up recent findings that temperature and precipitation are the major drivers of how sexual systems are spread across woody plant communities. They also suggest that we should not ignore spatial effects when we ask what shapes the mix of sexual systems.

So our results suggest that sexual systems are more than traits shaped by evolution. They are also working ecological indicators, because they tie a plant's reproductive strategy to its environment. Since sexual systems are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, tracking how often monoecious and dioecious species occur could tell us a lot about how forest communities are responding to ongoing climate change. This points to plant sexual systems as a new, trait-based way to monitor biodiversity as the world warms.

There is one more point to keep in mind. We counted species richness for each sexual-system category as an absolute number, and did not divide it by the total number of species in each plot. As a result, some of the geographic patterns we saw may partly reflect differences in overall diversity among plots, as well as real changes in the mix of sexual systems. Future studies that use richness-standardized measures, or that use relative abundance, may help separate these effects.

4.3.

How climate and terrain affect sexual systems differently in trees and shrubs

Our structural equation models show that climate and terrain were more strongly and significantly linked to the three sexual systems in trees than in shrubs (Figure 4). This is consistent with earlier large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Trees generally live longer and grow larger, and their parts above the ground are exposed to the weather for a long time. That may make them more sensitive to long-term environmental change (Wang et al., 2020a). This would explain why climate has a stronger effect on the geographic patterns of trees than of shrubs (Currie and Paquin, 1987). It also suggests that the difference in how climate shapes sexual systems in trees and shrubs may be linked to how each growth form gets and uses resources.

Our study has one limitation. We did not directly include how closely related the species are (their phylogenetic relatedness) in our analyses. Sexual systems often stay the same within a family tree of plants, so close relatives may share reproductive strategies simply because they share an evolutionary history. Some of the geographic patterns we saw may therefore partly reflect differences in which plant lineages live in each forest, or the history of how those lineages spread, and not only the environment sorting species. Future studies that include information on relatedness would help show how much evolutionary history and how much the environment each contribute to large-scale differences in the sexual systems of woody plants.

4.4.

How useful sexual systems could be for monitoring forests

Our findings suggest that the mix of sexual systems, especially the proportions of dioecious and monoecious species, may be a useful trait-based indicator of environmental conditions. Tracking changes in this mix could add helpful information to long-term forest monitoring programs such as ForestGEO and CForBio. Because the distribution of the different sexual systems was significantly linked to climate, watching for changes in the mix may show how forest communities respond to environmental variation.

However, our study compares places along climate gradients. It does not follow the same forests over time. So it does not directly test how well sexual systems work as indicators of ongoing climate change.

Common approaches such as remote sensing (observing forests from above) often focus on how green the canopy is, or on biomass. The mix of sexual systems could add insight into plants' reproductive strategies and into how communities come together. Still, monitoring sexual systems at a large scale needs long-term field observations and expert knowledge of plant types, which may limit its use for quick assessments. Future studies that combine sexual-system monitoring with remote sensing and trait databases may give us a fuller framework for tracking how biodiversity responds to environmental change.

parts.title: How tree and shrub reproductive systems change from south to north in Northern Hemisphere forests, and what drives these patterns
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

How plants arrange their male and female flower parts—their reproductive systems—helps shape how trees and shrubs live together and evolve. Yet we still do not fully understand how these systems vary across different climates.

Methods

We gathered information on 3,595 tree and shrub species from 30 marked forest areas used to track changes over time. These areas span tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions across the Northern Hemisphere. We examined broad patterns using three statistical methods: linear regression, which measures straight-line relationships; redundancy analysis, which links patterns across several measurements to environmental conditions; and structural equation modeling, which examines a network of proposed direct and indirect relationships.

Results

Farther north, a larger share of species had separate male and female flowers on the same plant, a system called monoecy. A smaller share had male and female flowers on different plants, a system called dioecy. Climate, especially temperature and precipitation—the amount of rain and snow—was the main driver of these opposite patterns.
