Environmental stress, including drought and extreme temperatures, may also change sex expression and reproductive investment by affecting plant physiology and interactions among plants (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016). For example, environmental conditions may change the relative costs and benefits of male and female reproductive roles, pollination success, or the balance of resources used for growth and reproduction. Together, these processes can shape which reproductive arrangements occur and persist in plant communities.

Geographic differences in plant reproductive arrangements may therefore reflect both broad patterns across latitude and the environmental gradients that occur along it.

Different environmental gradients reflect differences in habitat variety and available resources. Because latitude combines many climate and ecological factors, it is useful for examining broad biogeographic patterns in plant traits. Earlier studies have shown that traits linked to plant reproductive strategies change systematically along environmental gradients (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). Even so, we still do not know whether woody plant reproductive arrangements show consistent geographic patterns across forest communities in tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. Answering this question will help us understand how reproductive strategies respond to environmental differences across large areas.

The link between reproductive arrangement and plant growth type has received the most attention (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier research has confirmed that traits related to reproductive arrangement, such as life style, evolutionary age, and seed quality, are distributed along environmental gradients (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). Therefore, closely related reproductive arrangements may also follow patterns along gradients of environmental resources.

A study of 491 flowering-plant genera by Vamosi et al. (2003) found that species with male and female plants separate are more strongly associated with woody life forms, especially trees, than species with male and female flowers on one plant. Comparative studies of temperate forests in Sri Lanka and China have also confirmed this ecological link (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). A study of 19,780 flowering plants in China by Wang et al. (2020a) showed that the number of species with different reproductive arrangements differed between woody and herbaceous species. It also showed that the relative importance of different influences—especially climate, evolutionary age, and mature plant height—varied among growth forms.

Trees and shrubs generally have taller canopies, longer life spans, and greater reproductive investment than herbaceous plants. These features make them more likely to accumulate genetic changes over time. Differences in evolutionary rates may therefore contribute to differences in how climate niches evolve among growth forms (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014). Within woody plants, trees and shrubs also differ greatly in canopy height, longevity, ways of obtaining resources, and reproductive investment. These ecological differences may lead to different responses in the mix of reproductive arrangements along environmental gradients. Studying the geographic distribution and environmental drivers of reproductive arrangements in trees and shrubs will therefore improve our understanding of broad biogeographic patterns in plant reproductive strategies.

Here, we used reproductive-arrangement data for 3,595 woody species from 30 forest communities to examine large-scale patterns in woody plant reproductive arrangements and the main environmental factors linked with them along the latitudinal gradient. Climate and environmental conditions differ from low to high latitudes. Our 30 forest communities included humid and dry climates, plateau and plain landscapes, cold temperate regions in the north with seasonal temperatures, and tropical climates and landscapes in the south. This range allowed us to assess geographic patterns in vegetation reproductive arrangements across a wide set of environmental gradients.

We addressed three questions: (1) What latitudinal patterns do plant reproductive arrangements show across the 30 forest communities? (2) How do the distributions of different reproductive arrangements respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in reproductive-arrangement diversity along latitudinal gradients, and which environmental factors are most strongly associated with these patterns?
parts.methods:
## 2. Materials and methods

### 2.1. Study sites

For the past three decades, the Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO; https://forestgeo.si.edu/what-forestgeo) has collected long-term, large-scale forest data from tropical, subtropical, and temperate forests (Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio; http://www.cfbiodiv.org) has also expanded the CTFS network by setting up large mapped plots along a latitude gradient across temperate, subtropical, and tropical forests.

We used 20 plots from ForestGEO and 10 from CForBio. The two datasets were independent, with no plots in common. All 30 study sites were large forest dynamics plots covering at least 20 hectares. We focused on Northern Hemisphere plots because there were few comparable long-term forest plots with complete information on reproductive arrangements in the Southern Hemisphere.

We compared the reproductive arrangements of trees and shrubs across a latitude gradient in these 30 forest communities (Figure 1a). The plots ranged from 0.2918° N to 61.3000° N and from 56 to 1,902 m above sea level. They contained between 11 and 408 species, including some of the world’s most species-rich forests, such as Xishuangbanna (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). These differences in climate and geography can affect how plant reproductive arrangements change among forest plots. In every plot, data included the number of individual trees and trunk measurements for stems at least 1 cm in diameter at breast height (DBH). We included only trees and shrubs and excluded other growth forms, such as lianas and palms.

**Figure 1.** Global distribution of the 30 forest plots. Plot size ranged from 20 ha in Xishuangbanna to 120 ha in Mpala. Latitude ranged from 0.2918° N in Mpala, Republic of the Congo, to 61.3° N in Scotty Creek, Canada. The plots cover forests in Asia, Europe, and North America (a). The figure also shows species richness for different reproductive arrangements in forest communities from different climate zones (b) and an NMDS comparison of species composition among the 30 communities (c).

### 2.2. Reproductive-arrangement and environmental data

We collected reproductive-arrangement information for 3,595 species from the 30 permanent monitoring plots. To reduce species-recording errors caused by differences in time, region, and researchers, we checked all species names against *Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae* (1959–2004) and eFloras (http://efloras.org/). When different sources gave conflicting information about a species’ reproductive arrangement, we checked and corrected the records repeatedly.

The reproductive arrangement of some species can change with local living and non-living conditions, such as climate or pollinator density (Barrett and Harder, 2017; Schoen, 1982). We excluded these species from the analyses. Based on growth form, we divided woody plants into trees and shrubs.

We compiled information on reproductive arrangements from the *Flora of China* (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2; accessed May 2020), eFloras, and Tree of Sex (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we placed species into three groups. Hermaphroditic species have functional stamens and pistils in the same flower. Dioecious species have unisexual flowers, with female and male flowers on separate individual plants; this group also included androdioecy, gynodioecy, and trioecy. Monoecious species also have unisexual flowers, but male and female flowers occur on the same individual plant; this group included andromonoecy, gynomonoecy, and trimonoecy.

For each plot, we collected its latitude and longitude, topographic conditions, and climate conditions. Topographic data included mean slope (MS, °), mean elevation (ME, m), highest elevation (HA, m), and lowest elevation (LE, m). Climate data included mean annual precipitation (MAP, mm), precipitation in the wettest month (PWM, mm per month), precipitation in the driest month (PDM, mm per month), mean annual temperature (MAT, °C), and mean temperatures in the warmest (MTWM, °C) and coldest months (MTCM, °C).

We obtained plot locations and topographic information from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and CForBio. When these sources did not provide topographic information, we used topographic maps from the biodiversity monitoring network and calculated the measures following Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004). Climate data came from ForestGEO or published studies (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

For each forest plot, we described reproductive arrangements in two complementary ways. First, we calculated the proportion of species that were monoecious, dioecious, or hermaphroditic. This showed how community reproductive arrangements changed across the latitude gradient (Figure 1). Second, we counted the number of species in each reproductive-arrangement group. We used these species-richness values to examine links between reproductive-arrangement diversity and latitude, climate, and topography (Figure 2).

**Figure 2.** Relationships between species richness and environmental variables for woody plant reproductive arrangements in 30 plots. We used a spatial linear model, which examines relationships while accounting for the fact that nearby places may be more alike than distant places. Reproductive-arrangement species richness was the outcome, and climate, topographic factors, and latitude were the explanatory variables; the model included autoregressive errors. From right to left, the three rows show all species, trees, and shrubs. From top to bottom, the five columns show latitude, mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean elevation (ME), and mean slope (MS).

### 2.3. Data analysis

We included latitude, mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation, mean elevation, and mean slope in our analyses because earlier studies show that climate—especially temperature and rainfall—and topographic variation strongly affect plant reproductive traits and community composition. We calculated the proportion of species in each woody plant reproductive-arrangement group for all 30 forest communities using the species records from each community. We used alluvial diagrams, made with the “ggalluvial” package (Brunson, 2020), to show how these arrangements differed among climate zones. We also showed differences in species richness among the reproductive-arrangement groups graphically.

We used non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) to compare woody plant communities. NMDS places communities as points in a simplified space: communities with more similar species are closer together, while communities with more different species are farther apart (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). We used the stress value to judge how well the NMDS pattern represented the data and whether the arrangement model was reasonable. We ranked woody plant abundance in the 30 plots with NMDS and used fitted circles to show differences in forest-community species structure among climate zones.

We used linear regression to examine how latitude and environmental conditions were related to woody plant reproductive arrangements. Linear regression estimates how an outcome changes as one or more explanatory factors change. The outcomes were the numbers of monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic species. The explanatory variables were latitude, mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation, mean elevation, and mean slope. We analyzed species richness as the actual number of species and did not adjust it for the total number of species in each plot.

We used variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis to check whether the explanatory variables overlapped too strongly with one another (Supplementary Table 1). All VIF values were below 10, showing acceptable levels of overlap. We used adjusted R² to show how much variation in species turnover was explained by environmental variables (Tang et al., 2012). To avoid overestimating effects because we included many explanatory variables, we compared sample information criterion values and selected the best environmental model and spatial model separately.

We also used redundancy analysis (RDA), a method that combines regression with principal component analysis to summarize how environmental conditions relate to patterns in community data (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). The response data were the abundances of species in the three woody plant reproductive-arrangement groups. The explanatory data included longitude and latitude; topographic factors, including MS, ME, HA, and LE; and climate factors, including MAP, PWM, PDM, MAT, MTWM, and MTCM. Using 999 random permutations, we used the “envfit” function to examine how environmental factors were related to the distribution of woody plant reproductive arrangements across communities.

To compare further how non-living factors—latitude, terrain, and climate—affected reproductive-arrangement patterns, we built a structural equation model (SEM). This method uses linked regression relationships to examine direct and indirect connections among variables (Grace, 2006). We assumed that the overall effects of non-living factors directly affected reproductive-arrangement patterns and that latitude, MAT, PWM, MTWM, and MS could affect these patterns directly or indirectly. The full path model included an internal model, describing relationships among underlying variables, and an external model, describing relationships between these variables and measured indicators. In our study, the underlying variable was species richness of woody plant reproductive arrangements, and the measured variables were environmental factors.

We included covariances among monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic species richness in the SEM. Together, these groups describe the reproductive-arrangement structure of a community and are not statistically independent. Two-way arrows in the model show covariance, meaning that variables change together, rather than a cause-and-effect relationship.

We carried out all analyses in R 4.0.3 (R Core Development Team2). We created alluvial diagrams with “ggalluvial” (Brunson, 2020), performed NMDS and RDA with “vegan” (Oksanen et al., 2010), and performed SEM with “lavaan” (Rosseel Y et al., 2012).
parts.results:
## 3. Results

### 3.1. Sexual-system patterns across latitude

We examined the reproductive arrangements of woody plants across 30 forest plots in tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. Across these plots, the proportion of species with male and female flowers on one plant generally increased at higher latitudes. In contrast, hermaphroditic species showed the opposite pattern. The proportion of species with male and female plants separate remained relatively stable along the latitudinal gradient (Figure 1b). Together, these patterns suggest that the mix of reproductive arrangements changes systematically among climate zones.

An NMDS analysis, a method for comparing the species present in different communities, showed statistically significant differences in species composition among the 30 forest communities (Bray–Curtis stress = 0.031; Figure 1c).

Figure 1a shows where the 30 forest plots were located. They ranged from 0.29°N at Mpala, Republic of the Congo, to 61.3°N at Scotty Creek, Canada. Plot areas ranged from 20 ha to 120 ha. Figure 1b shows the proportions of species with male and female flowers on one plant, male and female plants separate, and hermaphroditic species across climate zones. Figure 1c shows differences in species composition among forest communities from the NMDS analysis.

We included only Northern Hemisphere plots because comparable long-term forest-dynamics plots with complete information on reproductive arrangements were limited in the Southern Hemisphere.

### 3.2. Effects of non-living environmental factors on sexual-system species richness

The number of hermaphroditic species was more strongly related to latitude and mean annual temperature (MAT) than the number of species with male and female flowers on one plant or male and female plants separate. For hermaphroditic plants, the adjusted R² values were 0.413 for all woody plants, 0.511 for trees, and 0.412 for shrubs. For species with male and female flowers on one plant, they were 0.181, 0.412, and 0.100, respectively. For species with male and female plants separate, they were 0.353, 0.419, and 0.310, respectively (Figure 2).

The statistically significant relationship between mean annual temperature and the number of species was stronger than the relationship with latitude for species with male and female flowers on one plant and for species with male and female plants separate. For monoecious plants, the adjusted R² was 0.421 for MAT (P < 0.001), compared with 0.181 for latitude (P < 0.001). For dioecious plants, the adjusted R² was 0.544 for MAT (P < 0.005), compared with 0.343 for latitude (P < 0.001).

The species richness of all three reproductive arrangements was significantly negatively related to latitude and significantly positively related to MAT (Figure 2). For both trees and shrubs, species richness was most strongly related to latitude and MAT, followed by mean annual precipitation (MAP). Mean slope and mean elevation (ME) showed the weakest relationships.

Links between species richness and topographic conditions—mean elevation and mean slope—were generally weak compared with links to climate conditions. However, some statistically significant relationships appeared for particular reproductive arrangements and plant forms (Figures 2d and 2e).

For species with male and female flowers on one plant, male and female plants separate, and hermaphroditic species, environmental variables explained 7.57%, 8.45%, and 7.37% of the variation in sexual-system community structure, respectively. Redundancy analysis (RDA), a method for showing how community differences relate to environmental conditions, indicated that longitude and MAT were the most important factors for all three groups. Precipitation in the wettest month (PWM) was also an important factor affecting all three reproductive arrangements. Climate factors were more important for tree reproductive arrangements, whereas longitude was more important for shrub reproductive arrangements (Figure 3).

Figure 3

RDA plot showing communities of species with male and female flowers on one plant, male and female plants separate, and hermaphroditic species across plant life forms. Ellipses show the 95% confidence interval. Asterisks show relationships between communities and environmental factors: *** indicates the strongest relationship (P < 0.001), ** indicates a strong relationship (P < 0.01), and * indicates a relationship (P < 0.05). MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, precipitation of the wettest month; PDM, precipitation of the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

### 3.3. Effects of climate on sexual-system species richness

In the structural equation model (SEM), which estimates links among several factors at the same time, climate factors—MAT, MTWM, and PWM—were positively related to the species richness of all three reproductive arrangements. The climate path coefficients were 0.88 for species with male and female flowers on one plant, 0.70 for species with male and female plants separate, and 0.77 for hermaphroditic species. These values were greater than the path coefficients linking the three reproductive arrangements with topographic and spatial factors (Figure 4).

Among different plant forms, the climate path coefficient for dioecious trees was 0.88, lower than the value for dioecious shrubs, 0.96. In contrast, the climate path coefficients for dioecious shrubs (0.81) and hermaphroditic shrubs (0.90) were higher than those for trees (0.75 and 0.57, respectively) (Figure 4). The SEM results show that the reproductive-arrangement groups responded differently to environmental variables. Compared with the dioecious group, the monoecious group had a more significant relationship with environmental variables.

Figure 4

This path diagram shows links among climate—temperature (MAT) and precipitation (MTWM and PWM)—topography (MS), space (latitude), and sexual-system species richness. Numbers beside arrows are standardized path coefficients. Red values show negative relationships, and blue values show positive relationships. Wider arrows show stronger relationships. *** indicates P < 0.001, ** indicates P < 0.01, and * indicates P < 0.05.
parts.discussion:
## 4. Discussion

We found a clear pattern in how many species had different reproductive arrangements across latitude in forest communities from different regions. These broad patterns differed among reproductive-arrangement categories and between trees and shrubs. Climate variables explained a substantial share of this variation.

### 4.1. How plant reproductive arrangements change from the equator toward the poles

We compared the proportions of plants with different reproductive arrangements in forests across tropical, subtropical, and temperate latitudes. In East Asia and North America, the proportion of hermaphroditic species—species with male and female reproductive parts in the same flower—did not increase or decrease significantly with latitude. In contrast, the proportion of species with male and female plants separate increased as latitude decreased, meaning that they were more common closer to the equator. The opposite trends for species with male and female flowers on one plant and species with male and female plants separate create strong geographic differences across the overall latitudinal gradient (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006).

Overall, the proportion of species with male and female flowers on one plant increased with latitude, whereas the proportion of species with male and female plants separate decreased with latitude. This suggests that the proportions of these two reproductive arrangements may be closely linked with region, especially latitude. However, hermaphroditic plants did not show a clear regular pattern across latitude (Chen and Li, 2008).

Earlier studies found more species with male and female plants separate than species with male and female flowers on one plant in low-latitude tropical regions (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also supported our findings: many low-density tropical tree species had a higher proportion of species with male and female plants separate. More recently, however, Wang et al. (2021) examined nearly 70,000 flowering-plant species worldwide and confirmed that both species with male and female plants separate and species with male and female flowers on one plant occur more often at high latitudes. Other studies have found that species with male and female plants separate are more common at high Northern Hemisphere latitudes. Research in North America and Siberia found that their proportion increases with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017).

The current spatial pattern of reproductive arrangements in flowering plants may result from the wider environmental tolerance and stronger ability to spread of plants with male and female plants separate and plants with male and female flowers on one plant. Our findings may also be related to the fact that we used the first species census data collected from these large plots. They are therefore consistent with earlier work by other researchers (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

### 4.2. How climate affects the richness of reproductive arrangements

In plant reproductive ecology, reproductive arrangements and the mating patterns they create are highly sensitive to changes in climate and geographic conditions (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). Our results show that hermaphroditic plants were more strongly linked with latitude and mean annual temperature (MAT) than were plants with male and female flowers on one plant or plants with male and female plants separate. For trees and shrubs in all three reproductive-arrangement categories, the strongest links were with latitude and MAT (Figure 2).

Climate conditions, including temperature and rainfall, can affect which reproductive arrangement a plant expresses. They can do this by changing plant physiology and ecology and by affecting reproductive performance during flowering (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). In our best models, variables representing temperature and rainfall explained the proportion of species in all three reproductive-arrangement categories among all species, tree species, and shrub species (Figure 4). Topography, mean annual precipitation (MAP), precipitation in the driest month (PDM), and mean temperature of the coldest month (MTCM) may also affect geographic differences in the proportions of reproductive arrangements among all species, trees, and shrubs. However, their effects were weaker than those of MAT and precipitation in the wettest month (PWM).

These findings suggest that climate factors are the main drivers of the makeup and diversity of reproductive arrangements. This may be because continuing climate changes, such as less rainfall and warmer winters, can shift plant timing, including earlier flowering (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). Differences in the resources needed by male and female functions can then further affect population structure, local community makeup, and even the geographic distribution of reproductive-arrangement diversity (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Other findings support studies of the factors that shape species composition in forest communities at different scales (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study of how environmental stress affects sex ratios in flowering plants found a significant link between the proportions of species with male and female flowers on one plant or on separate plants and climate factors, including temperature and rainfall (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). In summary, our results support recent findings that temperature and rainfall are major drivers of where reproductive arrangements occur in woody plant communities. They also suggest that spatial effects should not be ignored when interpreting the factors that shape reproductive-arrangement composition.

Our results therefore suggest that reproductive arrangements are not only evolutionary traits. They can also act as functional ecological indicators that connect plant reproductive strategies with environmental conditions. Because they are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, tracking changes in the frequencies of species with male and female flowers on one plant and species with male and female plants separate could offer useful clues about how forest communities are responding to ongoing climate change. This highlights the potential of plant reproductive arrangements as a new trait-based measure for monitoring biodiversity under global warming.

In addition, we analyzed the number of species in each reproductive-arrangement category as an absolute number, rather than adjusting it for the total number of species in each plot. As a result, some geographic patterns we observed may partly reflect differences in overall community diversity among plots, as well as changes in reproductive-arrangement composition. Future studies that use measures adjusted for total species richness or relative abundance may help separate these effects.

### 4.3. How non-living environmental factors affect trees and shrubs with different reproductive arrangements

Our structural equation model, which tests linked relationships among factors, showed that climate and topographic factors were more strongly linked with the three reproductive arrangements in trees than in shrubs (Figure 4). This agrees with earlier large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Trees generally live longer and grow larger than shrubs. Their aboveground tissues remain exposed to climate conditions for longer periods, which may make them more sensitive to long-term environmental variation (Wang et al., 2020a). Climate therefore has a stronger effect on the spatial pattern of trees than on that of shrubs (Currie and Paquin, 1987). These results suggest that differences in how climate affects the geographic patterns of reproductive arrangements in trees and shrubs may also be linked with differences in how these growth forms obtain and use resources.

One limitation of our study is that we did not directly include how closely related species are in evolutionary history in our analyses. Plant reproductive arrangements are often conserved across related species, meaning that closely related groups may share similar reproductive strategies because of their shared history. Therefore, some geographic patterns we observed may partly reflect differences in which evolutionary lineages occur in forest communities, or past biogeographic processes, rather than environmental filtering alone. Future studies that include evolutionary relationships would help separate the contributions of evolutionary history and environmental factors to broad-scale variation in woody plant reproductive arrangements.

### 4.4. The potential value of plant reproductive arrangements for monitoring

Our findings suggest that the composition of reproductive arrangements, especially changes in the proportions of species with male and female plants separate and species with male and female flowers on one plant, may be a useful trait-based environmental signal. Tracking changes in reproductive-arrangement composition may add useful information to long-term forest-monitoring programs such as ForestGEO and CForBio. Because the distribution of different reproductive arrangements was significantly linked with climate variables, monitoring changes in their composition may provide additional information about how forest communities respond to environmental variation.

However, our study is based on spatial links across climate gradients, rather than observations through time. It therefore does not directly test how well reproductive arrangements work as indicators of ongoing climate change. Traditional methods such as remote sensing often focus on canopy greenness or biomass. Reproductive-arrangement composition may offer additional insight into plant reproductive strategies and the processes that shape community makeup. However, monitoring reproductive arrangements across large areas requires long-term field observations and taxonomic expertise, which may limit its use in rapid assessments. Future studies that combine reproductive-arrangement monitoring with remote sensing and trait-based databases may provide a more complete framework for tracking how biodiversity responds to environmental change.

parts.title: How woody plants’ reproductive systems vary with latitude and climate in Northern Hemisphere forests
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

A plant’s reproductive system is an important trait that affects the ecology and evolution of woody plant communities. Yet we still know little about how these systems vary across different climates.

Methods

We gathered information on 3,595 woody plant species from 30 forest plots across tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. We used several statistical methods to study large-scale patterns and their relationships with environmental conditions.

Results

The proportion of species with male and female flowers on the same plant increased with latitude, while the proportion of species with male and female flowers on separate plants decreased. Climate, especially temperature and precipitation, was the main factor associated with these patterns. Climate relationships were stronger for trees than for shrubs.

Discussion

Our results show that the kinds of reproductive systems found in woody plant communities vary across geographic and climate gradients. The consistent changes in the proportions of these species highlight the ecological importance of reproductive systems and suggest that they may help us understand how forest communities respond to environmental change. Long-term studies are needed to assess whether these traits can help monitor ongoing climate change.

Keywords: climate change, ecological indicator, latitudinal gradient, sexual systems, woody plants
parts.introduction_first:
Species diversity generally decreases from the equator toward the poles, making latitude one of the major patterns in the geography of life. We see this pattern in forest communities across different climate zones (Rosenzweig, 1995). Flowers are part of a plant’s reproductive system. A plant’s sexual system describes how its flowers produce female and male reproductive parts. These systems include monoecy, dioecy, and more complex forms (Cardoso et al., 2018; Yampolsky and Yampolsky, 1922). In monoecious plants, the same individual has separate male and female flowers; in dioecious plants, male and female flowers grow on different individuals. A plant’s sexual system affects how it reproduces, which can shape the genetic features and evolutionary path of its populations (Barrett, 1992; Fox, 1985; Sabath et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020a). Sexual systems therefore matter for how plant communities and ecosystems form and persist (Chen and Li, 2008; Ibarra‐Manríquez and Oyama, 1992).

Sexual systems may both reflect how plants respond to environmental change and influence how forest ecosystems evolve across regions (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Charlesworth, 2006; Campbell and Kessler, 2013). Earlier research has found strong latitude-related patterns in plant diversity and community makeup, with notable differences among regions such as East Asia and North America (Boufford and Spongberg, 1983; Wang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2017). Most of this work has examined the number of species, the variety of species, or other plant traits. Much less attention has been given to reproductive traits across whole communities. Sexual systems are important to plant reproduction, population change, and evolution, yet we know little about how woody plant sexual systems vary across large areas—especially in forests spanning tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. This gap makes it harder to understand how reproductive strategies vary with climate and respond to environmental change.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We mapped how often different reproductive systems occur among woody plants in 30 forest communities across different latitudes, and compared how nonliving environmental conditions relate to their frequency. The proportions of monoecious and dioecious plants changed along the latitude gradient. Trees and shrubs differed significantly in how often their sexual systems occurred and in the factors linked to them. These findings show a relationship between the sexual systems in forest communities and environmental conditions across latitudes.

Together, our results reveal large-scale geographic patterns in woody plant sexual systems and highlight their potential as practical ecological indicators for assessing and predicting climate-driven ecosystem change. Adding changes in sexual systems to long-term forest monitoring may greatly improve our ability to detect, understand, and reduce climate change impacts on biodiversity.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent research suggests that where different reproductive systems occur in plants may depend on several biological and environmental factors. These include whether plants are trees or shrubs, their reproductive traits, climate, and their evolutionary history (Chazdon et al., 2003; Queenborough et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020b). Researchers often compare places at different latitudes to study broad ecological patterns because temperature and rainfall change systematically across these regions. But latitude does not directly affect plants; it stands in for several environmental changes that occur from the equator toward the poles.

Climate can directly affect how plants develop their reproductive parts, when they flower, and how they use resources. These effects may influence which reproductive systems occur and where they are found (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Gougherty and Gougherty, 2018; Inouye et al., 2019). Stressful conditions, such as drought and extreme temperatures, may also change how plants express their sex and how much they invest in reproduction. They do so by affecting plants’ ability to function and the ways plants interact with one another (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016). For example, environmental conditions may change the costs and benefits of male and female reproductive functions, affect pollination success, or shift how plants divide resources between growth and reproduction. In turn, these processes may shape which reproductive systems occur and persist in plant communities.

Thus, geographic differences in plant reproductive systems may reflect both broad patterns across latitudes and the environmental changes linked to latitude.

Environmental gradients reflect differences in habitat variety and available resources. Because latitude brings together several climatic and ecological factors, it offers a useful way to study broad geographic patterns in plant traits. Earlier studies have found that traits linked to plant reproductive strategies change in consistent ways across environmental gradients (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). However, we still know little about whether trees and shrubs show consistent geographic patterns in forest communities across tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. Answering this question will help us understand how reproductive strategies respond to environmental differences across large areas.

Researchers have paid most attention to the relationship between reproductive system and plant growth type (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier studies have shown that traits linked to reproductive systems—including life style, evolutionary age, and seed quality—vary along environmental gradients (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). This suggests that plant reproductive systems, which are closely linked to these traits, may also follow patterns across environmental resources.

A study of 491 angiosperm genera found that plants with male and female flowers on separate plants were more often woody, especially trees, than plants with male and female flowers on the same plant (Vamosi et al., 2003). Studies comparing temperate forests in Sri Lanka and our country have also found this relationship (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). In a study of 19,780 angiosperm species in China, Wang et al. (2020a) found that the number of species with different reproductive systems varied between woody plants and herbs. They also found that the influence of different factors—especially climate, evolutionary age, and adult plant height—varied between these growth types.

Trees and shrubs are usually taller, live longer, and invest more in reproduction than herbs. Over time, these differences may make woody plants more likely to accumulate genetic changes. Differences in the pace of evolution may therefore help explain why growth types differ in how their climate preferences evolve (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014). Trees and shrubs also differ from each other in height, lifespan, ways of obtaining resources, and investment in reproduction. These differences may lead them to respond differently to environmental gradients. Studying where reproductive systems occur in trees and shrubs, and which environmental factors are linked to them, will help us understand broad geographic patterns in plant reproductive strategies.

We examined data on reproductive systems in 3,595 species of trees and shrubs across 30 forest communities to explore broad patterns along latitude and identify the main environmental factors linked to them. From lower to higher latitudes, the communities span different climates and environmental conditions: they range from humid to dry settings and from plateaus to plains, as well as from cold-temperate regions in the north, with strong seasonal temperature changes, to tropical regions in the south. This range of conditions allows us to examine geographic patterns in plant reproductive systems across many environmental gradients.

We asked three questions: (1) How do plant reproductive systems vary across latitude in the 30 forest communities? (2) How do the distributions of different reproductive systems respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in reproductive-system diversity across latitude, and which environmental factors are linked to these patterns?

## 2. Materials and methods

### 2.1. Study site

For more than three decades, the Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO) has collected long-term data from large forest plots in tropical, subtropical, and temperate forests (Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio) has also expanded the CTFS network and set up large mapped plots across temperate, subtropical, and tropical forests along a north–south gradient. We used 20 plots from ForestGEO and 10 from CForBio. The datasets are independent and do not share any plots. Each study plot was a large forest dynamics plot covering at least 20 ha.

We focused on Northern Hemisphere plots because comparable long-term forest plots with complete information on plant reproductive systems were limited in the Southern Hemisphere. We compared the reproductive-system composition of trees and shrubs in 30 forest communities across a change from the equator toward the poles (Figure 1a). The plots ranged from 0.2918° N to 61.3000° N in latitude and from 56 to 1902 m in elevation. Species counts ranged from 11 to 408. The plots include some of the world’s most species-rich forests, such as Xishuangbanna (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). These broad differences in climate and location affect changes in the reproductive systems found in forest plots.

All plots recorded the number of individual trees and trunk measurements for stems at least 1 cm in diameter at breast height (DBH). We studied only trees and shrubs, excluding other growth forms such as lianas and palms.

**Figure 1.** Locations of the 30 forest plots. Plot sizes range from 20 ha (Xishuangbanna) to 120 ha (Mpala), and latitudes range from 0.2918° N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3° N (Scotty Creek, Canada). The plots cover forests in Asia, Europe, and North America (a). Panel b shows the species richness of forest-community reproductive systems in different climate zones. Panel c shows an NMDS analysis of species composition across the 30 communities.

### 2.2. Reproductive systems and environmental data

We gathered information on 3,595 species from the 30 permanent monitoring plots. To reduce errors in species records that could arise from differences in time, location, or researchers, we checked all species names against *Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae* (1959–2004) and eFloras (http://efloras.org/). We repeatedly checked and corrected conflicting records of species’ reproductive systems from different sources. Some species’ reproductive systems may vary with local living or nonliving conditions, such as climate or pollinator density (Barrett and Harder, 2017; Schoen, 1982). We left those species out of the analyses. We grouped the plants by growth form as trees or shrubs.

We identified species’ reproductive systems using *Flora of China* (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2; accessed May 2020), eFloras, and Tree of Sex (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we grouped reproductive systems into three categories. Hermaphroditic species have functional male and female parts in the same flower. In dioecious species, male and female flowers are on separate individuals; this category also includes androdioecy, gynodioecy, and trioecy. In monoecious species, male and female flowers are on the same individual; this category also includes andromonoecy, gynomonoecy, and trimonoecy.

For each plot, we used its latitude and longitude, topography, and climate. Topography measures included mean slope (MS, °), mean elevation (ME, m), highest elevation (HA, m), and lowest elevation (LE, m). Climate measures included mean annual precipitation (MAP, mm), precipitation in the wettest month (PWM, mm per month), precipitation in the driest month (PDM, mm per month), mean annual temperature (MAT, °C), and mean temperatures in the warmest (MTWM, °C) and coldest (MTCM, °C) months.

We obtained plot locations and topographic measurements from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and CForBio. When these networks did not provide some topographic measurements, we obtained them from topographic maps in the biodiversity monitoring network. We calculated them using the methods of Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004). Climate data came from ForestGEO or published studies (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

We measured the reproductive-system composition of each forest plot in two ways. First, we calculated the proportion of species that were monoecious, dioecious, or hermaphroditic to describe how community composition changed across the latitude gradient (Figure 1). Second, we counted the species in each reproductive-system category to examine how species richness related to environmental conditions, including latitude, climate, and topography (Figure 2).

**Figure 2.** Relationships between species richness in different woody-plant reproductive-system groups and environmental measures across the 30 plots. The spatial linear model used reproductive-system richness as the outcome and climate, topography, and latitude as explanatory variables, with autocorrelated errors. The rows show all species, trees, and shrubs, respectively. The five columns show latitude, mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean elevation (ME), and mean slope (MS), respectively.

### 2.3. Data analysis

We chose latitude, mean annual temperature (MAT), mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean elevation (ME), and mean slope (MS) for analysis because earlier studies have shown that climate—especially temperature and precipitation—and variation in land shape are major factors linked to plant reproductive traits and community composition. For each of the 30 forest communities, we calculated the proportions of species in each woody-plant reproductive-system group from the species records. We used the “ggalluvial” package to draw alluvial diagrams showing reproductive-system composition across climate zones (Brunson, 2020), and we graphed differences in species richness among reproductive-system groups.

Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) represents communities as points in a space with several dimensions. The distance between two points shows how different the communities are (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). We used the stress value to judge how well the NMDS results fit the data and whether the arrangement was suitable. We used NMDS to arrange the woody-plant abundance data from the 30 plots and drew circles to show differences in species composition among forest communities in different climate zones.

We used linear regression to examine how latitude and environmental conditions related to woody-plant reproductive systems. The outcomes were the numbers of monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic species; the explanatory variables were latitude, MAT, MAP, ME, and MS. We analyzed the actual species counts, without adjusting them for the total number of species in each plot. We checked variance inflation factors (VIFs) to see whether explanatory variables were too closely related to one another (Supplementary Table 1). All VIF values were below 10, indicating acceptable levels of overlap among the variables. We used adjusted R², a measure of how much variation the model explains while accounting for the number of variables, to represent the proportion of variation in species turnover explained by environmental variables (Tang et al., 2012). To avoid overestimating effects by including many explanatory variables, we compared sample information criterion values and selected the best environmental model and the best spatial model separately.

Redundancy analysis (RDA) combines regression with principal component analysis to summarize patterns in data (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). Our response data were the abundance of species in the three woody-plant reproductive-system groups. The explanatory data were environmental measurements: longitude and latitude; topography (MS, ME, HA, and LE); and climate (MAP, PWM, PDM, MAT, MTWM, and MTCM). We used the “envfit” function and 999 random permutations to examine how environmental conditions related to the distribution of woody-plant reproductive-system groups across communities.

To compare how nonliving environmental conditions related to reproductive-system patterns, we built a structural equation model (SEM). We assumed that the overall effects of nonliving conditions directly affected reproductive-system patterns, while latitude, MAT, PWM, MTWM, and MS could affect those patterns directly or indirectly. An SEM is a statistical method based on regression models (Grace, 2006). Its complete path model includes an internal model describing relationships between potential variables and an external model describing relationships between measured indicators. In our model, the potential variable was the richness of woody-plant reproductive systems, and the measured variables were environmental conditions. We included covariances among the richness of monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic species because the three groups jointly describe community reproductive-system composition and are not statistically independent. Two-way arrows represent covariance, not cause-and-effect relationships.

We conducted all analyses in R 4.0.3. We made alluvial diagrams with “ggalluvial” (Brunson, 2020), carried out NMDS and RDA with “vegan” (Oksanen et al., 2010), and performed SEM with “lavaan” (Rosseel Y et al., 2012).
parts.results:
## 3. Results

### 3.1. How reproductive systems vary across latitude

We studied the reproductive systems of woody plants in 30 forest plots across tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. Across the plots, the share of species with male and female flowers on the same plant generally increased with latitude. The share of species with male and female flowers on separate plants changed little, while the share of hermaphroditic species showed the opposite pattern to monoecious species (Figure 1b). These patterns suggest that the mix of reproductive systems varies across climate zones.

The species composition differed significantly among the 30 forest communities in an NMDS analysis, a method that displays how different communities are from one another (Bray–Curtis stress = 0.031; Figure 1c). Figure 1a shows where the plots were located, from 0.29°N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3°N (Scotty Creek, Canada); plot sizes ranged from 20 ha to 120 ha. Figure 1b shows the proportions of monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic species across climate zones. Figure 1c shows differences in species composition among the forest communities. We included only Northern Hemisphere plots because comparable long-term forest plots with complete reproductive-system information were limited in the Southern Hemisphere.

### 3.2. How nonliving conditions relate to reproductive-system richness

The number of hermaphroditic species was more strongly related to latitude and mean annual temperature (MAT) than the number of monoecious or dioecious species, across all plants and among trees and shrubs (Figure 2). For hermaphroditic plants, adjusted R² values were 0.413 for all plants, 0.511 for trees, and 0.412 for shrubs. For monoecious plants, they were 0.181, 0.412, and 0.100, respectively; for dioecious plants, they were 0.353, 0.419, and 0.310.

For monoecious and dioecious plants, richness was more strongly related to MAT than to latitude. For monoecious plants, adjusted R² was 0.421 for MAT (P < 0.001) and 0.181 for latitude (P < 0.001). For dioecious plants, it was 0.544 for MAT (P < 0.005) and 0.343 for latitude (P < 0.001). Richness in all three reproductive systems was significantly negatively related to latitude and significantly positively related to MAT (Figure 2). Across trees and shrubs, richness in each reproductive system was most strongly related to latitude and MAT, followed by mean annual precipitation (MAP); relationships with slope and mean elevation (ME) were weakest. Overall, relationships with topographic conditions—mean elevation and mean slope—were weak compared with relationships with climate, although some significant links appeared for particular reproductive systems and plant growth forms (Figures 2d, e).

Environmental conditions explained 7.57% of the variation in the mix of reproductive systems among monoecious plants, 8.45% among dioecious plants, and 7.37% among hermaphroditic plants. Redundancy analysis (RDA), which relates community patterns to environmental conditions, showed that longitude and MAT were the most important factors for all three reproductive systems. Precipitation in the wettest month (PWM) was also important for all three. Climate was more important for the reproductive systems of trees, while longitude was more important for shrubs (Figure 3).

**Figure 3.** RDA plot showing monoecious, dioecious, and hermaphroditic communities across plant growth forms. Ellipses show 95% confidence intervals. Asterisks mark relationships between communities and environmental conditions: *** P < 0.001 (strongest), ** P < 0.01 (strong), and * P < 0.05. MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, precipitation in the wettest month; PDM, precipitation in the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; and MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

### 3.3. How climate relates to reproductive-system richness

In our structural equation model (SEM), climate conditions—MAT, MTWM, and PWM—were positively related to the richness of all three reproductive systems. The climate path coefficients were 0.88 for monoecious plants, 0.70 for dioecious plants, and 0.77 for hermaphroditic plants. Each was greater than the coefficients for topographic and spatial conditions (Figure 4).

The climate relationship also differed between trees and shrubs. For dioecious plants, the climate path coefficient was lower for trees (0.88) than for shrubs (0.96). For shrubs, the coefficients were higher than for trees for dioecious plants (0.81 compared with 0.75) and hermaphroditic plants (0.90 compared with 0.57) (Figure 4). The SEM results show that the reproductive-system groups responded differently to environmental conditions. The relationship between environmental conditions and the monoecious group was stronger than the relationship with the dioecious group.

**Figure 4.** Diagram showing how climate (temperature: MAT and MTWM; precipitation: PWM), topography (MS), and location (latitude) relate to reproductive-system richness. Numbers beside arrows are standardized path coefficients. Red numbers show negative relationships and blue numbers show positive relationships. Wider arrows show stronger relationships. Asterisks mark paths: *** P < 0.001, ** P < 0.01, and * P < 0.05.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

Our study found clear changes with latitude in the numbers of species with different reproductive systems across forest communities. These broad patterns differed among reproductive-system types and between trees and shrubs. Climate explained a substantial part of this variation.

4.1.

How reproductive systems vary from the equator toward the poles

We compared the proportions of species with different reproductive systems in forests across tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions. Across the latitude gradient, the proportion of species with male and female flowers on the same plant did not increase or decrease significantly in East Asia or North America. By contrast, the proportion of species with male and female flowers on separate plants increased as latitude decreased. The opposing patterns for these two reproductive systems create strong geographic differences across the full latitude gradient (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006). Overall, the proportion of species with male and female flowers on the same plant increased with latitude, while the proportion with male and female flowers on separate plants decreased. This suggests that the proportions of these two groups may be closely related to region, especially latitude. Species with both male and female reproductive parts in their flowers, however, showed no clear pattern across the latitude gradient (Chen and Li, 2008).

Earlier studies found more species with male and female flowers on separate plants than species with male and female flowers on the same plant in low-latitude tropical regions (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also reported, in line with our findings, that many tropical tree species occurring at low density have a higher proportion of species with male and female flowers on separate plants. However, Wang et al. (2021) recently studied nearly 70,000 flowering-plant species worldwide and found that both groups—species with male and female flowers on separate plants and those with male and female flowers on the same plant—occur more often at high latitudes. Other studies have found that species with male and female flowers on separate plants are more common at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere. Studies in North America and Siberia have also found that their proportion increases with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017).

The current geographic patterns of reproductive systems in flowering plants may be linked to the broad range of conditions these plants can tolerate and their ability to spread. Our data came from the first species surveys of these large forest plots, and our findings are consistent with earlier studies (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

4.2.

How climate relates to reproductive-system richness

In plant reproduction research, reproductive systems and the mating patterns they shape are highly sensitive to changes in climate and geography (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). Our results show that the proportions of species with male and female reproductive parts in the same flower were more strongly related to latitude and average annual temperature than the proportions of the other two reproductive-system groups. For all three groups, the relationships with latitude and average annual temperature were strongest for trees and shrubs (Figure 2).

Temperature and precipitation can also affect which reproductive system a plant expresses by changing its physical and ecological traits and by influencing how well it reproduces during flowering (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). In our best-fitting models—the statistical models that best matched the data—temperature and precipitation measures helped explain the proportions of species in each of the three reproductive-system groups, both across all species and separately for trees and shrubs (Figure 4). Landform, mean annual precipitation, precipitation during the driest month, and mean temperature in the coldest month may also affect geographic differences in these proportions among all species, trees, and shrubs, respectively. But their effects were weaker than those of average annual temperature and precipitation in the warmest month. These results suggest that climate is a main driver of the mix and diversity of reproductive systems. Ongoing climate changes, such as less rainfall and warmer winters, may also change plant timing, such as causing earlier flowering (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). Differences in the resources needed for male and female reproduction may then further affect population structure, the local mix of reproductive systems, and even where this diversity occurs (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Other studies of forest species composition at different scales support our findings (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study of how environmental stress affects the balance of male and female plants in flowering plants found that the proportions of species with male and female flowers on the same plant and those with flowers on separate plants were strongly related to climate, including temperature and precipitation (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). Overall, our results support recent findings that temperature and precipitation are major drivers of reproductive-system patterns in woody plant communities. They also suggest that we should consider geographic location when interpreting the factors that shape these patterns.

Our results suggest that reproductive systems are more than traits shaped by evolution: they can also act as useful ecological indicators, linking plant reproduction strategies with environmental conditions. Because they are sensitive to temperature and precipitation, tracking changes in the proportions of species with male and female flowers on the same plant and those with flowers on separate plants may help show how forest communities respond to ongoing climate change. This points to the potential of reproductive systems as a new way to monitor biodiversity using plant traits as the climate warms.

We measured the number of species in each reproductive-system group as a raw total, rather than adjusting it for the total number of species in each plot. So some geographic patterns may partly reflect differences in overall species diversity among plots, as well as changes in the mix of reproductive systems. Future studies could use measures adjusted for total species richness or measures of relative abundance to help separate these effects.

4.3.

How nonliving conditions relate to reproductive-system richness in trees and shrubs

The results of our model showed that climate and landform were more strongly related to the reproductive systems of trees than to those of shrubs (Figure 4). This agrees with previous large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Trees and shrubs generally live longer and grow larger than other plants. Their aboveground parts remain exposed to climate for a long time, which may make them more sensitive to long-term environmental changes (Wang et al., 2020a). Climate therefore has a stronger effect on the geographic patterns of woody plants than on shrubs (Currie and Paquin, 1987). Differences in how climate relates to reproductive-system patterns in trees and shrubs may also reflect differences in how these growth forms acquire and use resources.

One limitation of our study is that we did not include how closely related the species are in our analyses. Reproductive systems are often shared among related plant species, which may have similar reproductive strategies because of their shared evolutionary history. Some of the geographic patterns we observed may therefore partly reflect differences in the species’ evolutionary lineages or past geographic history among forest communities, rather than environmental conditions alone. Future studies that include evolutionary relationships among species could help separate the contributions of evolutionary history and environmental factors to broad patterns in woody plant reproductive systems.

4.4.

How reproductive systems could help monitor forests

Our findings suggest that the mix of reproductive systems—especially changes in the proportions of species with male and female flowers on separate plants and those with flowers on the same plant—may be a useful indicator of environmental conditions. Tracking changes in this mix could add useful information to long-term forest monitoring programs such as ForestGEO and CForBio. Because the distribution of reproductive systems was strongly related to climate, monitoring these changes may also help show how forest communities respond to environmental variation.

However, our study compared locations across climate gradients; it did not track changes over time. It therefore does not directly test how well reproductive systems indicate ongoing climate change. Unlike common approaches such as remote sensing, which often track how green forest canopies are or how much plant material they contain, reproductive-system patterns may offer additional insight into plant reproduction strategies and how communities form. Still, monitoring reproductive systems across large areas requires long-term field observations and taxonomic expertise, which may make this approach harder to use for rapid assessments. Future studies combining reproductive-system monitoring with remote sensing and databases of plant traits may provide a more complete way to track how biodiversity responds to environmental change.

parts.title: How the way trees and shrubs reproduce changes from the equator toward the poles, and what drives it, in forests of the Northern Hemisphere
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

Plants can be arranged in different ways when it comes to making seeds. Some have both male and female flowers on the same plant, some have male and female flowers on separate plants, and some have more complicated arrangements. We call these arrangements a plant's "sexual system." Sexual systems are key features of woody plants (trees and shrubs) that shape how their communities live and how they change over time. Yet we still do not understand well how these systems change as the climate changes from place to place.

Methods

We gathered information on 3,595 woody plant species from 30 large forest plots. These plots are areas of forest where scientists record the trees and shrubs over many years. Together they cover tropical, subtropical and temperate forests across the Northern Hemisphere. To look for large-scale patterns, we used three statistical tools. Linear regression measures how one thing changes as another changes. Redundancy analysis looks at how a whole set of environmental conditions lines up with a whole set of plant features. Structural equation modeling tests a network of possible links between many factors at once.

Results

The share of species with both male and female flowers on the same plant went up as we moved farther from the equator. The share of species with male and female flowers on separate plants went down. So these two groups showed opposite trends. Climate was the main driver of these patterns, especially temperature and rainfall. The links between climate and sexual systems were stronger in trees than in shrubs.

Discussion

These results show that differences in how woody plants reproduce from place to place are closely tied to changes in climate. Monoecious and dioecious species (the two groups above) changed in a consistent way as conditions changed. This shows that sexual systems matter for how forests work. It also suggests that they may give us useful information about plant features for understanding how forest communities respond to environmental change. More long-term studies are needed to find out whether they could help us keep watch on forests as the climate keeps changing.

Keywords: climate change, ecological indicator, latitudinal gradient, sexual systems, woody plants
parts.introduction_first:
One of the most important patterns on Earth is that the number of species drops as you travel from the equator toward the poles. This pattern shows up in forests in many different climate zones (Rosenzweig, 1995).

Flowers are part of a plant's reproductive system. Scientists sort plants' sexual systems into three main types. In monoecious plants, both male and female flowers grow on the same plant. In dioecious plants, male and female flowers grow on different plants. Some plants have even more complicated systems (Cardoso et al., 2018; Yampolsky and Yampolsky, 1922).

A plant's sexual system affects how it reproduces. That, in turn, affects the genetic makeup of its populations and the direction in which they evolve (Barrett, 1992; Fox, 1985; Sabath et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020a). So sexual systems play an important part in how plant communities and whole ecosystems are built and kept going (Chen and Li, 2008; Ibarra‐Manríquez and Oyama, 1992). They do more than show how plants respond to a changing environment. They also shape how forest ecosystems evolve across a whole region (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Charlesworth, 2006; Campbell and Kessler, 2013).

Earlier studies have found clear changes in plant diversity and in which species make up a community as you move from the equator toward the poles. They have also found big differences between regions such as East Asia and North America (Boufford and Spongberg, 1983; Wang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2017). Most of these studies, however, looked at how many species there are, how varied the groups of plants are, or other plant features. They paid fairly little attention to how plants' reproductive features vary across whole communities.

Among these features, sexual systems play a basic role in how plants reproduce, how their populations grow and shrink, and how they evolve. Even so, we still know little about how the sexual systems of woody plants are spread across large areas. This is especially true for forests that stretch from the tropics, through the subtropics, to the temperate regions. This gap in knowledge holds back our understanding of how plants' ways of reproducing change as the climate changes, and how they respond to environmental change.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We mapped how often each type of sexual system appears in woody plants across 30 forest communities at different latitudes in different regions. We also compared how non-living parts of the environment, such as climate and the shape of the land, affect how common each type is.

We found that the share of monoecious plants (both male and female flowers on the same plant) and dioecious plants (male and female flowers on separate plants) changed as we moved from the equator toward the poles. Trees and shrubs differed in a statistically significant way, both in how common each type was and in what shaped it. (A difference is called statistically significant when a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no difference.) These findings shed light on how the sexual systems of forest communities relate to environmental factors as you move from the equator toward the poles.

Taken together, our study reveals large-scale patterns in how woody plants reproduce. It also shows that these patterns could be used as practical ecological indicators, meaning measurable signs that help us assess and predict how ecosystems change as the climate changes. Adding changes in sexual systems to long-term forest monitoring may greatly improve our ability to detect, understand and reduce the effects of climate change on the variety of life on Earth.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent evidence suggests that how a plant's sexual system varies from place to place depends on many biological and environmental factors. These include the plant's life form (for example, whether it is a tree, a shrub or a herb), its reproductive features, the climate, and the history of how the plant has grown and developed over its life (Chazdon et al., 2003; Queenborough et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020b).

Scientists often study changes from the equator toward the poles to look for large-scale patterns in nature. This is because climate changes in a steady, predictable way along this direction, with temperature and rainfall shifting step by step. Latitude itself, however, does not directly cause anything in nature. Instead, it works as a stand-in for many environmental changes that happen together as you move across the globe.

Climate may directly affect how a plant's reproductive parts develop, when it flowers, and how it shares out its resources. In these ways, climate may affect which sexual systems appear and where they are found (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Gougherty and Gougherty, 2018; Inouye et al., 2019). Harsh conditions such as drought and extreme temperatures may also change how much a plant puts into male or female reproduction. They do this by affecting how well the plant's body works and how it interacts with other plants (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016). For example, conditions may change the costs and benefits of being male or female, change how well a plant is pollinated, or change how much it puts into growing compared with reproducing. In the end, these processes can shape which sexual systems appear in a plant community and how long they last there.

So the way sexual systems vary from place to place may reflect both the broad pattern of change from the equator toward the poles and the environmental changes that come with it.

Different environmental changes reflect differences in how varied the habitats are and how many resources are available. Because latitude brings together many climate and ecological factors, it gives us a useful way to study large-scale patterns in plant features. Earlier studies have shown that features linked to how plants reproduce change in a steady way along these environmental changes (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). Even so, we still know very little about whether the sexual systems of woody plants follow the same geographic patterns in forest communities across the tropics, subtropics and temperate regions. Answering this question will help us understand how plants' ways of reproducing respond to environmental change over large areas.

The link between a plant's sexual system and its growth type (whether it is a tree, a shrub or a herb) has received the most attention (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier studies have confirmed that features related to sexual systems, such as a plant's life style, its evolutionary age (how long ago its group of species split off from its relatives) and the quality of its seeds, are spread along environmental changes (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). So sexual systems, which are closely tied to these features, may also follow certain geographic patterns as resources change from place to place.

Several studies point in this direction. Vamosi et al. (2003) studied 491 genera of flowering plants. (A genus is a group of closely related species.) They found that dioecious plants are more often woody, especially trees, than monoecious plants. Studies comparing temperate forests in Sri Lanka and in our country have confirmed this link (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). Wang et al. (2020a) studied 19,780 flowering plant species in China. They found that the mix of sexual systems differed between woody plants and herbs. They also found that the importance of different drivers, especially climate, evolutionary age and the height of the fully grown plant, varied between growth types.

Woody plants usually have taller crowns, live longer and put more into reproduction than herbs do. This makes them more likely to build up genetic changes over time. Differences in how fast they evolve may therefore help explain why growth types differ in how their climate niches (the range of climates they can live in) have evolved (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014). Among woody plants, trees and shrubs also differ a great deal in crown height, how long they live, how they gather resources and how much they put into reproduction. These differences may mean that the mix of sexual systems in trees and in shrubs responds differently to environmental changes. So studying where sexual systems are found in trees and shrubs, and what drives them, will help us understand large-scale patterns in how plants reproduce.

In this study, we used information on the sexual systems of 3,595 woody plant species from 30 forest communities. We looked for large-scale trends in woody plant sexual systems as we moved from the equator toward the poles, and for the main environmental factors driving them. The climate and other conditions change in different ways as you move from low latitudes to high latitudes. Our 30 forest communities covered a wide range of conditions. They ranged from wet to dry climates and from high plateaus to flat plains. They also ranged from cold temperate zones in the north, where the seasons set the temperature, to tropical climates and landscapes in the south. This wide range lets us study geographic patterns in plant communities across many environmental changes.

We set out to answer three questions. (1) How do plant sexual systems change from the equator toward the poles across the 30 forest communities? (2) How do the different sexual systems respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in the variety of sexual systems as we move from the equator toward the poles, and what are the main environmental factors linked to these patterns?
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

Where we did the study

Over the past thirty years, the Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO; https://forestgeo.si.edu/what-forestgeo) has been collecting long-term, large-scale data on forests in the tropics, subtropics and temperate regions (Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio; http://www.cfbiodiv.org) has also added to the CTFS network, a worldwide network of forest plots. It has set up large mapping plots that run from temperate forests, through subtropical forests, to tropical forests.

We took twenty plots from ForestGEO and ten from CForBio. The two sets of data are independent, and no plot appears in both. Every plot we used is a large forest dynamics plot, meaning an area of forest of at least 20 hectares where scientists record the trees and shrubs over many years. (A hectare is a square 100 meters on each side.)
