We focused on forest plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there are few long-term forest plots that record every species' sexual system. So we compared the mix of sexual systems among woody plants in 30 forest communities from these two networks, spread along a line from the equator toward the poles (Figure 1a).

The plots lie between 0.2918° N and 61.3000° N, at heights from 56 to 1902 meters above sea level. Each plot holds between 11 and 408 species, and some of them, such as the Xishuangbanna plots, are among the forests in the world with the most species (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). These big differences in climate and geography affect how the sexual systems of plants in a forest plot change.

In every plot, we counted the individual trees and measured trunks at least 1 cm across at chest height (a measurement called DBH, for "diameter at breast height"). We looked only at trees and shrubs. We left out other kinds of woody plants, such as lianas (woody climbing vines) and palms.

Figure 1

Where the 30 forest plots are around the world. The plots range in size from 20 hectares (Xishuangbanna) to 120 hectares (Mpala). They range in latitude from 0.2918° N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3° N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and they cover forests in Asia, Europe and North America (a). The number of species in each sexual-system group in different climate zones (b). A map of how similar the species lists of the thirty communities are, made with a method called NMDS (c).

2.2.

Sexual systems and environmental data

We gathered information on 3,595 species from 30 permanent monitoring plots. Different researchers, working at different times and in different regions, sometimes record the same species under different names. To avoid this kind of mistake, we checked the species names in every community against the Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae (1959–2004), a major book of Chinese plants, and against eFloras (http://efloras.org/). When different sources gave conflicting sexual systems for the same species, we checked and corrected them again and again.

A species' sexual system can sometimes change depending on local living and non-living conditions, such as the climate or how many pollinators are around (Barrett and Harder, 2017) (e.g. Schoen, 1982). We left such species out of our analysis. Based on the kind of plant they are, we sorted the species into two types: trees and shrubs.

We took the sexual systems of the woody plants in our data from the Flora of China (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2, accessed in May 2020), from eFloras, and from Tree of Sex (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we sorted the sexual systems into three groups.

The first group is hermaphroditic species. These have both working stamens (the male parts) and pistils (the female parts) in the same flower. The second group is dioecious species, which have male and female flowers on different plants. This group includes androdioecy, gynodioecy and trioecy. The third group is monoecious species, which have male and female flowers on the same plant. This group includes andromonoecy, gynomonoecy and trimonoecy.

For each plot, we also collected information on its location (longitude and latitude), the shape of the land, and the climate. For the shape of the land, we used the average slope (MS, in degrees), the average height above sea level (ME, in meters), the highest point (HA, in meters) and the lowest point (LE, in meters). For the climate, we used the average yearly rainfall (MAP, in millimeters), the rainfall in the wettest month (PWM, in millimeters per month), the rainfall in the driest month (PDM, in millimeters per month), the average yearly temperature (MAT, in °C), and the average temperatures of the warmest month (MTWM, in °C) and the coldest month (MTCM, in °C).

We took the latitude, longitude and land-shape information from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and from the Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network. For some plots, these sources did not give the land-shape information. For those, we worked it out from topographic maps in the monitoring network, following the methods of Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004). We took the climate information from ForestGEO or from earlier studies (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

We described the sexual systems in each forest plot with two measures that complement each other. First, we worked out what share of the species in each community were monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic. This showed how the mix of sexual systems in a community changes as you move from the equator toward the poles (Figure 1). Second, we counted how many species fell into each sexual-system group. We used these counts to look at how the variety of sexual systems relates to the environment, including latitude, climate and the shape of the land (Figure 2).

Figure 2

How the number of species relates to different features of woody plant sexual systems in the 30 plots. We used a spatial linear model, a version of linear regression that allows for the fact that nearby plots tend to be alike. The number of species in each sexual-system group was the thing being explained. The explaining factors were climate, the shape of the land and latitude. The model also allowed for the way errors in nearby plots are linked (autoregressive errors). The three rows, from right to left, show all species, trees and shrubs. The five columns, from top to bottom, show latitude, average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average height above sea level (ME) and average slope (MS).

2.3.

How we analyzed the data

We chose the environmental factors in our analyses (latitude, average yearly temperature, average yearly rainfall, average height above sea level and average slope) because earlier studies have shown that they matter a great deal. Climate, especially temperature and rainfall, and differences in the shape of the land are major forces shaping how plants reproduce and which species make up a community.

We worked out the share of species in each sexual-system group in the 30 forest communities from the sexual-system information for the species recorded in each community. To show how the mix of sexual systems differs between climate zones, we drew alluvial diagrams with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). These are flow charts in which bands of color run from one column to the next, showing how species are split between groups. We also drew graphs of how the number of species differs between the sexual-system groups.

Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) is a way of drawing a map of how different communities are. It places each community as a point in a space with many dimensions, so that the distance between two points shows how different those communities are (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). We judged how well the NMDS map fits the data, and how reasonable the ranking is, using a number called the stress coefficient. A lower stress means a better fit. In this study, we ranked the woody plants in the 30 plots with NMDS and drew circles to show how the mix of species differs between forest communities in different climate zones.

We used linear regression to explore how moving from the equator toward the poles, and the environmental factors, affect the sexual systems of woody plants. The things we tried to explain were the number of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. The explaining factors were latitude, average yearly temperature, average yearly rainfall, average height above sea level and average slope. We used the actual number of species in each group, not the number divided by the total number of species in the plot.

Some environmental factors tend to rise and fall together, which can confuse a regression. To check for this, we used a test called the variance inflation factor (VIF) (Supplementary Table 1). All the VIF values were below 10, which shows that this problem was at an acceptable level.

To show how much of the change in the number of species the environmental factors could explain, we used a measure called adjusted R² (Tang et al., 2012). It gives the share of the variation that the model explains, adjusted for how many factors are in the model. Adding many factors can make a model look better than it really is. To avoid this, we compared models using a score called the sample information criterion, which rewards a model for fitting well but penalizes it for having too many factors. In this way, we chose the best environmental model and the best spatial model.

Redundancy analysis (RDA) combines regression with principal component analysis, a method that boils many measurements down to a few main patterns (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). In our analysis, the thing being explained was the number of species in each of the three woody plant sexual-system groups. The explaining factors were longitude and latitude, the shape of the land (average slope, average height, highest point and lowest point) and the climate (average yearly rainfall, rainfall in the wettest month, rainfall in the driest month, average yearly temperature, and the average temperatures of the warmest and coldest months). We used the "envfit" function to study how the environmental factors affect the way woody plant sexual systems are spread across communities. To test whether the links were stronger than chance would produce, we shuffled the data 999 times and compared the results with the shuffled ones.

We also wanted to compare more closely how non-living parts of the environment (latitude, the shape of the land and climate) affect the pattern of sexual systems. For this, we built a structural equation model (SEM). We assumed that the total effect of these non-living factors directly affects how sexual systems are spread out. We also assumed that latitude, average yearly temperature, rainfall in the wettest month, the average temperature of the warmest month and average slope affect the spread of sexual systems, either directly or indirectly.

The SEM we used is a statistical method based on regression (Grace, 2006). A complete path model has two parts. The internal model describes how the hidden factors relate to each other. The external model describes how the measured factors relate to those hidden factors. In our study, the hidden factor was the number of species in each woody plant sexual-system group, and the measured factors were the environmental factors.

We also included covariances among the numbers of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. A covariance measures how two things tend to rise and fall together. These three groups together describe the mix of sexual systems in a community, so they are not independent of each other. In the model, two-way arrows show these covariances, not cause-and-effect links.

We ran all the analyses in the statistics program R, version 4.0.3 (R Core Development Team2). We drew the alluvial plots with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We ran the NMDS and RDA with the "vegan" package (Oksanen et al., 2010), and the SEM with the "lavaan" package (Rosseel Y et al., 2012).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

A pattern in sexual systems that stretches from the equator toward the poles

We looked at how the sexual systems of woody plants are spread across 30 forest plots. Together, these plots cover tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. In general, the share of monoecious species (both male and female flowers on the same plant) went up as we moved farther from the equator. The share of hermaphroditic species showed the opposite pattern. Hermaphroditic plants have both male and female parts in the same flower. The share of dioecious species (male and female flowers on separate plants) stayed fairly steady from the equator toward the poles (Figure 1b). These trends suggest that the mix of sexual systems changes in a regular way across different climate zones.

To compare the species lists of the 30 forest communities, we used a method called NMDS (non-metric multidimensional scaling). It draws a kind of map in which communities with similar species sit close together and communities with very different species sit far apart. The species lists of the 30 communities differed in a statistically significant way (Figure 1c). The measure of how well this map fits the data, called the Bray–Curtis stress, was 0.031. A lower value means a better fit.

Figure 1 has three panels. Panel a shows where the 30 forest plots are. They range from 0.29°N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3°N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and each plot covers between 20 and 120 hectares. Panel b shows the share of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species in each climate zone. Panel c shows how the species lists of the forest communities differ, based on the NMDS analysis.

We included only plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there are few long-term forest plots that record every species' sexual system.

3.2.

How non-living parts of the environment affect the number of species in each sexual system

We first asked how the number of species in each sexual system relates to latitude and to climate. To measure how closely two things are linked, we used a number called R²adj. It runs from 0 to 1 and shows how much of the variation in one thing can be explained by the other. The higher it is, the stronger the link.

The number of hermaphroditic species was linked fairly strongly to latitude and to mean annual temperature (the average temperature over a year). This held for all woody plants together (R²adj = 0.413), for trees (0.511) and for shrubs (0.412). Monoecious plants were linked much more weakly (all woody plants: 0.181; trees: 0.412; shrubs: 0.100). Dioecious plants fell in between (all woody plants: 0.353; trees: 0.419; shrubs: 0.310) (Figure 2).

For monoecious and dioecious plants, the link with mean annual temperature was stronger than the link with latitude. For monoecious plants, the R²adj with temperature was 0.421, compared with 0.181 for latitude. For dioecious plants, it was 0.544, compared with 0.343. Both links with temperature were statistically significant (monoecious: P < 0.001; dioecious: P < 0.005). A P value below 0.001 means that if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would turn up by chance less than 0.1% of the time.

For all three sexual systems, the number of species went down as we moved farther from the equator, and this link was statistically significant. The number of species also went up as mean annual temperature rose, and this link was statistically significant too (Figure 2).

We also looked at trees and shrubs separately. For both, the number of species in each sexual system was most strongly linked to latitude and mean annual temperature. Next came mean annual precipitation (the average rainfall over a year). The weakest links were with the slope of the land and with mean elevation (the average height above sea level). In general, the links with the shape of the land were weaker than the links with climate. Even so, we found some statistically significant links for particular sexual systems and plant types (Figures 2d, e).

Next, we asked how much of the differences in the mix of sexual systems could be explained by the environment. We used redundancy analysis, which looks at how a whole set of environmental conditions lines up with a whole set of plant features. For monoecious plants, the environmental conditions explained 7.57% of the differences in the mix of sexual systems. For dioecious plants, they explained 8.45%, and for hermaphroditic plants, 7.37%.

The redundancy analysis showed that longitude and mean annual temperature were the most important factors for monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic plants. The rainfall of the wettest month was also an important factor for all three. For trees, climate mattered more. For shrubs, longitude mattered more (Figure 3).

Figure 3

Redundancy analysis of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic communities for different plant types. The ovals show the 95% confidence region, the area where the community is expected to fall. Stars show how each community relates to each environmental factor. "***" marks the strongest link (P < 0.001), "**" a strong link (P < 0.01) and "*" a link (P < 0.05). MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, rainfall of the wettest month; PDM, rainfall of the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

3.3.

How climate affects the number of species in each sexual system

Finally, we used structural equation modeling to test a network of possible links. In this model, each link gets a number called a path coefficient. The larger the number, the stronger the link.

The climate factors (mean annual temperature, mean temperature of the warmest month and rainfall of the wettest month) were positively linked with the number of species in all three sexual systems. Their path coefficients were 0.88 for monoecious plants, 0.70 for dioecious plants and 0.77 for hermaphroditic plants. These were larger than the path coefficients for the links between the three sexual systems and the shape of the land or latitude (Figure 4).

Trees and shrubs also differed. For dioecious plants, the path coefficient for climate was lower in trees (0.88) than in shrubs (0.96). For shrub dioecious plants (0.81) and hermaphroditic plants (0.90), it was higher than for trees (0.75 and 0.57) (Figure 4).

The structural equation model shows that the sexual systems respond differently to the environment. The link between the monoecious system and the environment was more statistically significant than the link between the dioecious system and the environment.

Figure 4

Path map showing how climate (temperature: mean annual temperature, MAT; rainfall: mean temperature of the warmest month, MTWM, and rainfall of the wettest month, PWM), the shape of the land (mean slope, MS) and latitude are linked to the number of species in each sexual system. The number next to each arrow is the path coefficient, scaled so the arrows can be compared. Red numbers show a negative link and blue numbers a positive link. Thicker arrows show stronger links. "***" marks a path with P < 0.001, "**" a path with P < 0.01 and "*" a path with P < 0.05.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

Our study showed a clear pattern as you move from the equator toward the poles: the number of species with each type of sexual system changed in different ways in different regional forest communities. These large-scale patterns were not the same for every type of sexual system, and they differed between trees and shrubs. Climate explained a large part of these differences.

4.1.

How the variety of sexual systems changes from the equator toward the poles

In this study, we compared the share of each type of sexual system in forests from the tropics, through the subtropics, to the temperate regions. In East Asia and North America, the share of species with both male and female flowers on the same plant did not go up or down in a statistically significant way as we moved from the equator toward the poles. In other words, we could not show a clear trend for this group. The share of species with male and female flowers on separate plants, however, went up as we moved farther from the equator.

Because these two groups trend in opposite directions, the balance between them changes a great deal from place to place along the whole range from the equator toward the poles (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006). Overall, our results show that the share of monoecious species rises with latitude, while the share of dioecious species falls as latitude rises. To some extent, this suggests that the shares of monoecious and dioecious species may be closely tied to the region, and especially to how far north it lies. The share of plants with both male and female flowers on the same plant, however, showed no clear regular pattern along this range (Chen and Li, 2008).

Early studies found more dioecious species than monoecious species in tropical regions near the equator (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also confirmed our finding that many tropical tree species that grow far apart from one another have a higher share of dioecious species. More recently, Wang et al. (2021) used nearly 70,000 species of flowering plants to study how sexual systems are spread across the whole world. They confirmed that both dioecious and monoecious species are more common at high latitudes, farther from the equator. Other studies have found that dioecious species are more common at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere. Studies in North America and Siberia found that the share of dioecious species rises with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017).

The way sexual systems are spread out today in flowering plants is due to the fact that dioecious and monoecious plants can cope with a wider range of conditions and can spread their seeds more easily. Our findings may also be linked to the fact that the data we used were the first species counts for these large plots, and so they agree with earlier studies by others (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

4.2.

How climate affects the number of species with each sexual system

In the study of how plants reproduce, a plant's sexual system, and the way it mates, are very sensitive to changes in climate and in the surrounding landscape (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). Our results show that plants with both male and female flowers on the same plant are more closely linked to latitude and to mean annual temperature (the average temperature over a year) than monoecious and dioecious plants are. For all three sexual systems, trees and shrubs are most strongly linked to latitude and mean annual temperature (Figure 2).

Climate, meaning temperature and rainfall, can also change how a plant's sexual system shows up. It does this by changing how the plant's body works and how it fits into its surroundings, and by controlling how well the plant reproduces while it is in flower (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). Our results suggest that measures of temperature and rainfall were chosen in the best models for explaining the share of species with each of the three sexual systems, for all species together, for trees and for shrubs (Figure 4).

Other factors may also affect how the share of each sexual system varies from place to place, for all species, for trees and for shrubs. These include the shape of the land, mean annual precipitation (the average amount of rain and snow in a year), PDM and MTCM. However, their effects are weaker than those of mean annual temperature and PWM. These findings suggest that climate should be the main driver of which sexual systems are present and how varied they are.

This may be because the climate is changing, for example with less rain and warmer winters, and because the timing of plant events is shifting, for example with earlier flowering (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). On top of this, monoecious and dioecious plants need different amounts of resources such as light, water and nutrients. These differences further affect how populations are made up, which species grow together in a place, and even where different sexual systems are found across the landscape (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Other findings agree with studies on what decides which species make up forest communities, at different scales (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study on how environmental stress affects the balance of males and females in flowering plants found a statistically significant link between the ratio of monoecious to dioecious species and climate factors (temperature and rainfall) (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). In short, our results confirm recent findings that temperature and rainfall are major drivers of where different sexual systems are found in communities of woody plants. They also suggest that the effects of location should not be ignored when we try to understand what shapes the mix of sexual systems.

Our results therefore suggest that sexual systems are not just features that plants inherited over long stretches of evolution. They are also working signs of how plants live, linking the way plants reproduce with the conditions around them. Because they are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, keeping track of changes in how common monoecious and dioecious species are could tell us a lot about how forest communities are responding to ongoing climate change. This shows that plant sexual systems could be a new, feature-based way to keep watch on the variety of life as the world warms.

We should also point out one limitation of how we counted species. We looked at the number of species with each sexual system as a plain count, rather than as a share of all the species in each plot. So some of the patterns we saw from place to place may partly come from differences in how many species each plot holds overall, and not only from changes in the mix of sexual systems. Future studies that use counts adjusted for the total number of species, or that measure how common each type is compared with the others, may help separate these two effects.

4.3.

How non-living parts of the environment affect the number of species with each sexual system, in trees and shrubs

Our structural equation model shows that climate and the shape of the land are more strongly linked to the three sexual systems of trees than of shrubs, and these links are statistically significant (Figure 4). This agrees with earlier large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009).

Woody plants usually live longer and grow bigger than other plants. Their parts above the ground stay out in the open, exposed to the weather for a long time, which may make them more sensitive to long-term changes in their surroundings (Wang et al., 2020a). So climate has a significant effect on where woody plants are found, compared with shrubs (Currie and Paquin, 1987). These results suggest that the different effects of climate on the sexual systems of woody plants and shrubs may also be linked to differences in how these two growth forms get and use resources.

One limitation of our study is that we did not directly take into account how closely related the species are through evolution. A plant's sexual system is often passed down within a family line, and closely related species may share similar ways of reproducing because they share a common history. So some of the patterns we saw from place to place may partly reflect differences in which family lines make up each forest community, or in how species arrived in different places over time, and not only the sorting of species by their environment. Future studies that include information on how species are related would help separate how much evolutionary history and how much the environment each contribute to large-scale differences in the sexual systems of woody plants.

4.4.

Could plant sexual systems help us keep watch on forests?

Our findings suggest that the mix of sexual systems, especially changes in how common dioecious and monoecious species are, may be a useful feature-based sign of environmental conditions. Keeping track of changes in this mix may add useful information to long-term forest monitoring programs such as ForestGEO and CForBio. Because where different sexual systems are found was significantly linked to climate, tracking changes in the mix may also add information on how forest communities respond to changes in their surroundings.

However, our study looks at how things are linked across places with different climates, not at how they change over time. So it does not directly test how well sexual systems work as signs of ongoing climate change. Traditional methods, such as remote sensing (taking pictures of the Earth from satellites), often focus on how green the treetops are or how much plant material there is. Compared with these, the mix of sexual systems may give extra insight into how plants reproduce and how communities come together. Still, keeping watch on sexual systems over large areas needs long-term field observations and experts who can identify species, which may limit its use for quick assessments. Future studies that combine monitoring of sexual systems with remote sensing and databases of plant features may give a fuller way to track how the variety of life responds to environmental change.

parts.title: How the mix of male and female plants in forests changes from the equator toward the North, and what drives it
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

Plants can reproduce in different ways. Some have both male and female parts on the same plant, some have separate male and female plants, and some have both in the same flower. Scientists call these arrangements a plant's "sexual system." These systems are key features that shape how groups of woody plants live together and how they evolve. Yet we still do not understand well how they change as the climate changes from place to place.

Methods

We gathered information on 3,595 species of woody plants (trees and shrubs) from 30 large forest plots. These plots are long-term research sites where scientists count and measure the plants growing there. Together they cover tropical, subtropical and temperate forests across the Northern Hemisphere, the half of the world north of the equator. To look for large-scale patterns, we used three statistical methods. Linear regression tests how one quantity changes along with another. Redundancy analysis tests how a whole set of environmental factors lines up with a whole set of plant features. Structural equation modeling tests a network of possible cause-and-effect links between many factors at once.

Results

The farther north a plot was, the larger the share of species with both male and female parts on the same plant. The share of species with separate male and female plants went the other way. So the two kinds of species showed opposite trends as we moved north. Climate was the main driver of these patterns, especially temperature and rainfall. The link between climate and sexual system was stronger in trees than in shrubs.

Discussion

Our results show that the way woody plants reproduce is closely tied to how the climate changes from place to place. The steady changes we saw in both kinds of species across different environments show that sexual systems matter for how forests work. They also suggest that sexual systems may be useful features for tracking how forest communities respond to environmental change. More long-term studies are needed to find out whether they could help us keep watch on forests as the climate keeps changing.

Keywords: climate change, ecological indicator, latitudinal gradient, sexual systems, woody plants
parts.introduction_first:
One of the most important patterns in nature is that the number of plant species drops as you travel from the equator toward the poles. This happens in forests in every climate zone (Rosenzweig, 1995).

Flowers are part of a plant's reproductive system, the part of the plant that makes seeds. Scientists sort plants into sexual systems, which describe how they reproduce. The main kinds are monoecious plants, which have both male and female parts on the same plant, dioecious plants, which have separate male and female plants, and some more complex systems (Cardoso et al., 2018; Yampolsky and Yampolsky, 1922).

A plant's sexual system affects how it reproduces. That, in turn, affects the genetic makeup of plant populations and the direction in which they evolve (Barrett, 1992; Fox, 1985; Sabath et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020a). Sexual systems therefore play an important part in how plant communities and whole ecosystems are built and kept going (Chen and Li, 2008; Ibarra‐Manríquez and Oyama, 1992). They do more than show how plants respond to environmental change. They also shape how forest ecosystems evolve across whole regions (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Charlesworth, 2006; Campbell and Kessler, 2013).

Earlier studies have found strong changes in plant diversity and in which plants make up a community as you move from the equator toward the poles. They also found large differences between regions such as East Asia and North America (Boufford and Spongberg, 1983; Wang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2017). Most of these studies, however, looked at how many species there are, at how many different groups of plants there are, or at functional traits, which are features such as height or leaf shape. Much less attention has gone to how the ways plants reproduce change across whole communities.

Among these reproductive features, sexual systems play a basic role in how plants reproduce, how their populations grow and shrink, and how they evolve. Even so, we still know little about how sexual systems of woody plants are spread across large areas of the world. This is especially true for forests that stretch from tropical to subtropical to temperate regions. That gap limits our understanding of how plants' ways of reproducing change as the climate changes, and how they respond to environmental change.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We mapped how common each sexual system of woody plants is across 30 forest communities at different latitudes in different regions. We then compared how non-living factors, such as climate and the shape of the land, affect how common each sexual system is.

We found that the share of plants with both male and female parts on the same plant, and the share of plants with separate male and female plants, changed as we moved from the equator toward the poles. Trees and shrubs also differed in how common each sexual system was and in what shaped it. These findings show how the sexual systems of forest communities relate to environmental factors as you move from the equator toward the poles.

Taken together, our study reveals large-scale patterns in how woody plants reproduce across the world. It also shows that sexual systems could be useful, practical ecological indicators: signs we can measure to assess and predict how ecosystems change as the climate changes. Adding changes in sexual systems to long-term forest monitoring may greatly improve our ability to detect, understand and reduce the effects of climate change on the variety of life.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent research suggests that sexual systems differ from place to place because of many biological and environmental factors. These include a plant's life form (for example, tree, shrub or herb), its reproductive features, the climate, and its history of growth and development (Chazdon et al., 2003; Queenborough et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020b).

Scientists often study large-scale patterns in nature by looking at how things change from the equator toward the poles. This is because latitude, meaning how far north or south a place is, is closely linked to steady changes in climate, such as temperature and rainfall. Latitude itself, however, does not directly drive what happens in nature. It is a stand-in for many other environmental changes that happen together. Climate factors may directly affect how a plant's reproductive parts develop, when it flowers, and how it shares out its resources. In this way, climate may affect where different sexual systems occur and how widely they are spread (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Gougherty and Gougherty, 2018; Inouye et al., 2019).

Stresses from the environment, such as drought and extreme temperatures, may also change how a plant expresses its sex and how much it puts into reproduction. They do this by affecting how well the plant's body works and how plants interact with one another (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016). For example, environmental conditions may change the costs and benefits of being male or female. They may also change how well a plant gets pollinated, or how it shares its resources between growing and reproducing. In the end, these processes can shape which sexual systems occur in a plant community and which ones last.

So the way sexual systems vary from place to place may reflect both broad patterns from the equator toward the poles and the environmental changes that lie behind them.

Different environmental changes reflect how varied a habitat is and how many resources, such as light, water and nutrients, are available. Because latitude brings together many climate and ecological factors, it is a useful way to study large-scale patterns in plant functional traits, the features that shape how plants live and grow. Earlier studies have shown that features linked to how plants reproduce change in a regular way along environmental changes (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). Still, we know very little about whether sexual systems of woody plants follow the same geographic patterns in forest communities across tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. Answering this question will help us understand how plants' ways of reproducing respond to environmental change over large areas.

The link between sexual system and plant growth type, meaning whether a plant is a tree, a shrub or an herb, has received the most attention (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier studies have confirmed that features related to sexual system, such as life style, evolutionary age (how long ago a plant's lineage split from others) and seed quality, are spread along environmental changes (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). So sexual system, which is closely related to these features, may also follow some pattern in space as resources change from place to place.

Vamosi et al. (2003) studied 491 genera of flowering plants. A genus is a group of closely related species. They found that plants with separate male and female plants were more often woody, especially trees, than plants with both male and female parts on the same plant. Studies comparing temperate forests in Sri Lanka and in our country have confirmed this link (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). Wang et al. (2020a) studied 19,780 flowering plants in China. They showed that the mix of sexual systems differed between woody and herbaceous species. They also showed that the importance of different drivers, especially climate, evolutionary age and the height of the mature plant, varied among growth forms.

Woody plants generally have taller canopies (the leafy tops of the plants), live longer and put more into reproduction than herbaceous species. This makes them more likely to build up genetic changes over time. Because different growth forms may evolve at different speeds, this may help explain why the way they evolve in response to climate differs (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014). Among woody plants, trees and shrubs also differ a great deal in canopy height, how long they live, how they gather resources and how they share out their reproduction. These ecological differences may lead to different responses in the mix of sexual systems as the environment changes. So studying where sexual systems occur in trees and shrubs, and what drives them, will improve our understanding of large-scale patterns in how plants reproduce.

In this study, we used information on sexual systems for 3,595 species of woody plants from 30 forest communities. We explored the large-scale pattern of woody plant sexual systems from the equator toward the poles, and the main environmental factors that drive it. The climate and other environmental conditions vary in different ways from low latitudes to high latitudes. The 30 forest communities we chose range from humid to dry climates and from high plateaus to low plains. They range from cold temperate zones, where the seasons are marked by temperature, in the north, to tropical climates and landscapes in the south. This lets us study how plant communities are arranged across a wide range of environmental changes.

In general, we set out to answer three questions: (1) How do sexual systems change from the equator toward the poles across the 30 forest communities? (2) How does the spread of different sexual systems respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in the variety of sexual systems from the equator toward the poles, and which environmental factors are most closely linked to these patterns?
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

Where we studied

Over the past thirty years, the Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO; https://forestgeo.si.edu/what-forestgeo) has collected long-term, large-scale data on forests in tropical, subtropical and temperate regions (Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio; http://www.cfbiodiv.org) has also grown the CTFS network, a worldwide network of forest plots. It has set up large mapping plots that stretch from temperate forests in the north, through subtropical forests, to tropical forests in the south.

We took twenty plots from ForestGEO and ten plots from CForBio. The two sets of data are independent, and none of the plots appear in both. Every plot we used was a large forest dynamics plot, meaning a plot where scientists count and measure the plants growing there, with an area of at least 20 hectares.

We focused on forest plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there were only a few long-term forest dynamics plots with complete information on sexual systems. So we compared the mix of sexual systems in woody plants along a north–south line, using 30 forest communities from these two networks (Figure 1a).

The plots lie between 0.2918° N and 61.3000° N, at heights of 56 to 1902 meters above sea level. The number of species in a plot ranges from 11 to 408. Some plots include some of the forests with the most species in the world, such as Xishuangbanna (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). These large differences in climate and geography affect how the sexual systems of plants in a plot change.

In every plot, we counted individual trees and measured trunks that were at least 1 cm across at breast height (DBH, the standard way of measuring trunk thickness). We looked only at trees and shrubs. We left out other kinds of plants, such as lianas (woody climbing vines) and palms.

Figure 1

Where the 30 forest plots are. The plots range in size from 20 hectares (Xishuangbanna) to 120 hectares (Mpala). They range in latitude from 0.2918° N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3° N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and they cover forests in Asia, Europe and North America (a). The number of species in each sexual system in different climate zones (b). A map of how the mix of species differs among the thirty communities, made with a method called NMDS (c).

2.2.

Sexual systems and environmental data

We gathered information on 3,595 species from 30 permanent monitoring plots. Different researchers, and records made at different times and in different regions, can name the same species in slightly different ways. To remove these recording errors, we checked the species names in every community against the Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae (1959–2004), a large book of plant names, and against eFloras (http://efloras.org/). Whenever different sources gave conflicting sexual systems for the same species, we checked and corrected them again and again.

A species' sexual system can also change depending on local living and non-living conditions, such as the climate or how many pollinators there are (Barrett and Harder, 2017; e.g. Schoen, 1982). In our analysis, we left these species out of the data. Based on how they grow, we sorted the plants into two types: trees and shrubs.

We took the sexual system of each woody plant from the Flora of China (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2, accessed in May 2020), eFloras and Tree of Sex (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we sorted the sexual systems into three groups.

The first group is hermaphroditic species, which have both working stamens (the male parts) and pistils (the female parts) in the same flower. The second group is dioecious species, which have separate male and female plants. In these species, the flowers are unisexual, meaning each flower is either male or female, and the female and male plants grow on different individuals. This group includes androdioecy, gynodioecy and trioecy. The third group is monoecious species, which have both male and female parts on the same plant. In these species, the flowers are unisexual, but the male and female flowers grow on the same individual. This group includes andromonoecy, gynomonoecy and trimonoecy.

For each plot, we also recorded its longitude and latitude. We also recorded features of the shape of the land: the average slope (MS, in degrees), the average height above sea level (ME, in meters), the highest point (HA, in meters) and the lowest point (LE, in meters). Finally, we recorded climate features: the average yearly rainfall (MAP, in millimeters), the rainfall in the wettest month (PWM, in millimeters per month), the rainfall in the driest month (PDM, in millimeters per month), the average yearly temperature (MAT, in °C), and the average temperature of the warmest month (MTWM, in °C) and the coldest month (MTCM, in °C).

We took the latitude, longitude and land-shape features from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and from the Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network. For plots where one of these organizations did not give land-shape features, we took them from the monitoring network's maps of the land, using the methods of Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004). We took the climate features from ForestGEO or from earlier studies (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

For each forest plot, we measured sexual systems in two ways that complement each other. First, we worked out the share of species in each sexual system: monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic. This showed how the mix of sexual systems in each community changes from the equator toward the poles (Figure 1). Second, we counted how many species belonged to each sexual system. We used these counts to look at how the variety of sexual systems relates to latitude, climate and the shape of the land (Figure 2).

Figure 2

How the number of species in each sexual system relates to different features in the 30 plots. We used a spatial linear model, a type of linear regression that allows for nearby plots being more alike than far-apart ones. The number of species in each sexual system was the outcome we were trying to explain. Latitude, climate, land-shape features and latitude were the possible explanations. The model also allowed for errors that are linked from one plot to the next (autoregressive errors). The three rows, from right to left, show all species, tree species and shrubs. The five columns, from top to bottom, show latitude, average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average height above sea level (ME) and average slope (MS).

2.3.

How we analyzed the data

We chose latitude, average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average height above sea level (ME) and average slope (MS) for our analyses. Earlier studies have shown that climate, especially temperature and rainfall, and differences in the shape of the land are major factors that decide how plants reproduce and which plants make up a community.

We worked out the share of species in each sexual system in the 30 forest communities from the sexual system data for the species recorded in each community. To show how the mix of sexual systems differs across climate zones, we drew alluvial diagrams, which are flow-like charts that join the groups together, using the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We also drew graphs of how the number of species differs among the sexual systems.

Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) is a method that turns many differences between communities into a simple map. Each community becomes a point, and the farther apart two points are, the more different those two communities are (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). We judged how well the map fits the data, and whether the ranking of communities makes sense, using a number called the stress coefficient. We ranked the 30 plots by how many woody plants they held using NMDS. We then drew circles to show how the mix of species differs between forest communities in different climate zones.

We used linear regression to explore how latitude and environmental factors affect the sexual systems of woody plants. The outcomes we were trying to explain were the number of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. The possible explanations were the environmental factors: latitude, average yearly temperature, average yearly rainfall, average height above sea level and average slope. We analyzed the number of species as a raw count, not as a share of all the species in the plot.

Some environmental factors tend to rise and fall together, which can confuse a regression. To check for this, we used a measure called the variance inflation factor (VIF) (Supplementary Table 1). All VIF values were below 10, which means the overlap between the factors was at an acceptable level.

We used the model-adjusted R² to show how much of the change in species turnover, meaning how much the mix of species changes from one plot to another, the environmental factors and other variables explain (Tang et al., 2012). Adding too many possible explanations can make a model look better than it really is. To avoid this, we compared several versions of the model using a score called the sample information criterion, which rewards a model for fitting the data well but penalizes it for being too complicated. We then chose the best environmental model and the best spatial model.

Redundancy analysis (RDA) is a method that combines regression with principal component analysis, a way of summing up many measurements in a few main patterns (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). In our analysis, the outcome data were the numbers of species in the three sexual systems. The explanation data were the environmental factors: longitude and latitude, the land-shape features (average slope, average height, highest point and lowest point), and the climate features (average yearly rainfall, rainfall in the wettest month, rainfall in the driest month, average yearly temperature, average temperature of the warmest month and average temperature of the coldest month). We used the "envfit" function to study how the environmental factors relate to the spread of the woody plant sexual systems. We ran 999 permutations, which means we shuffled the data 999 times to see how often a pattern this strong would appear by chance alone.

To compare more closely how non-living factors (latitude, the shape of the land and climate) affect the pattern of sexual systems, we built a structural equation model (SEM). We assumed that the non-living factors together have a direct effect on how the sexual systems are spread. We also assumed that latitude, average yearly temperature, rainfall in the wettest month, average temperature of the warmest month and average slope affect the spread of sexual systems, either directly or indirectly.

This SEM is a statistical method based on regression models (Grace, 2006). It has two parts. The internal model describes how the possible variables relate to each other. The external model describes how the measured variables relate to them. In our study, the possible variable is the number of species in each sexual system, and the measured variables are the environmental factors. We also included the covariances among the numbers of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species, meaning how much they tend to change together. These three groups together describe the mix of sexual systems in a community, and they are not statistically independent of each other. The arrows that point in both directions show covariances, not cause-and-effect relationships.

We ran all analyses in the statistics program R, version 4.0.3 (R Core Development Team). We made the alluvial diagrams with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020). We ran NMDS and RDA with the "vegan" package (Oksanen et al., 2010), and SEM with the "lavaan" package (Rosseel Y et al., 2012).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

A pattern of sexual systems that stretches from the equator toward the poles

We looked at how the sexual systems of woody plants are spread across 30 forest plots. These plots lie in tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. In most plots, the farther north we went, the larger the share of species with both male and female parts on the same plant. Species with both male and female parts on the same plant showed the opposite pattern. Species with separate male and female plants stayed at fairly steady shares along the whole range from south to north (Figure 1b). These trends suggest that the mix of sexual systems changes in a regular way from one climate zone to the next.

To compare the species in each plot, we used a method called NMDS. It draws a kind of map in which plots with similar species sit close together and plots with different species sit far apart. The 30 forest communities differed in which species they held, and these differences were statistically significant (Bray–Curtis stress = 0.031; Figure 1c). The stress value measures how much the flat map has to bend to fit the real differences, and a value this low means the map is a good fit.

Panel a of Figure 1 shows where the 30 forest plots are. They range from 0.29°N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3°N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and they cover areas from 20 to 120 hectares. Panel b shows the share of species with both male and female parts on the same plant, with separate male and female plants, and with both in the same flower in each climate zone. Panel c shows how the species in the forest communities differ, based on the NMDS map. We included only plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there were only a few long-term forest plots with complete information on sexual systems.

3.2.

How non-living factors affect the number of species in each sexual system

We first looked at species richness, which is simply the number of species of each sexual system in a plot. We measured how closely each number followed latitude and mean annual temperature (MAT), the average temperature over a whole year. To do this we used a measure called R²adj. It tells us how much of the ups and downs in the number of species a factor can account for, adjusted so that adding extra factors does not make the number look better than it really is.

The number of species with both male and female parts on the same plant was linked fairly strongly to latitude and mean annual temperature. This was true for all plants together (R²adj = 0.413), for trees (R²adj = 0.511) and for shrubs (R²adj = 0.412). The number of species with both male and female parts on the same plant was linked less strongly to latitude and mean annual temperature. This was true for all plants together (R²adj = 0.181), for trees (R²adj = 0.412) and for shrubs (R²adj = 0.100).

The number of species with separate male and female plants followed a similar pattern. It was linked more strongly to mean annual temperature than to latitude. For all plants together, the R²adj was 0.353 for mean annual temperature and 0.181 for latitude. For trees it was 0.419 and 0.412, and for shrubs it was 0.310 and 0.100.

These links with mean annual temperature were statistically significant. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. For the number of species with both male and female parts on the same plant, the P value was below 0.001. For the number of species with separate male and female plants, it was below 0.005.

For all three sexual systems, the number of species went down as latitude increased, and it went up as mean annual temperature increased. Both of these links were statistically significant (Figure 2).

We also compared the three kinds of plants: trees, shrubs and herbs. For trees and shrubs, the number of species in each sexual system was most strongly linked to latitude and mean annual temperature. Next came mean annual precipitation (MAP), the average amount of rain and snow over a year. The weakest links were with mean slope (ME), the average steepness of the land, and with mean elevation (MS), the average height of the land.

The links between the number of species and the shape of the land were generally weak compared with the links to climate. Even so, we found some statistically significant links for particular sexual systems and kinds of plants (Figures 2d, e).

Next we asked how much of the change in the mix of sexual systems in a plot could be explained by the environment. For species with both male and female parts on the same plant, the environmental factors explained 7.57% of the changes. For species with separate male and female plants, they explained 8.45%, and for species with both in the same flower, they explained 7.37%.

Redundancy analysis showed that longitude and mean annual temperature were the most important factors for all three sexual systems. Precipitation in the wettest month (PWM) was also an important factor for all three. For trees, climate factors mattered more. For shrubs, longitude mattered more (Figure 3).

Figure 3

Redundancy analysis map of the communities of species with both male and female parts on the same plant, with separate male and female plants, and with both in the same flower, for different kinds of plants. The ellipses show the 95% confidence interval, the area where the true center of each group is likely to lie. “*” marks the links between the community and environmental factors. “* * *” means the strongest link (P < 0.001), “**” means a strong link (P < 0.01), and “*” means a link (P < 0.05). MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, precipitation of the wettest month; PDM, precipitation of the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

3.3.

How climate affects the number of species in each sexual system

We used structural equation modeling to test a network of possible cause-and-effect links. In this model, each arrow has a number called a path coefficient. It shows how strongly one factor is linked to another, on a scale where larger numbers mean stronger links.

In the model, three climate factors were positively linked to the number of species in each of the three sexual systems. These were mean annual temperature (MAT), the mean temperature of the warmest month (MTWM) and precipitation in the wettest month (PWM). The path coefficients for species with both male and female parts on the same plant (0.88), species with separate male and female plants (0.70) and species with both in the same flower (0.77) were all greater than those for the links with the shape of the land and with space (Figure 4).

The kind of plant also made a difference. For species with separate male and female plants, the path coefficient for climate was lower in trees (0.88) than in shrubs (0.96). For species with both in the same flower, the path coefficient for climate was higher in shrubs (0.81) and in herbs (0.90) than in trees (0.75; 0.57) (Figure 4).

The model shows that the groups of species with each sexual system respond to the environment in different ways. The group of species with both male and female parts on the same plant had a more significant link with the environment than the group of species with separate male and female plants.

Figure 4

The path map shows how climate [temperature (MAT) and precipitation (MTWM and PWM)], the shape of the land (MS), space (latitude) and the number of species in each sexual system are linked. The number next to each arrow is the path coefficient, put on a common scale so the arrows can be compared. Red values show a negative link and blue values show a positive link. The thicker the arrow, the stronger the link. “* * *” means P < 0.001, “* *” means P < 0.01 and “*” means P < 0.05.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

Our study showed a clear pattern as you move from the equator toward the poles: the number of species with each sexual system changed in different forest communities in different regions. These large-scale patterns differed between the kinds of sexual systems and between trees and shrubs. Climate explained a large part of the differences we saw.

4.1.

How the mix of sexual systems changes from the equator toward the poles

In this study, we compared the share of each sexual system in forests at different latitudes in the tropics, the subtropics and the temperate zones. In East Asia and North America, the share of species with both male and female parts on the same plant did not rise or fall in a statistically significant way as we moved north. (A result is called statistically significant when a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no link. "Not significant" means we could not show a link, not that there is none.) The share of species with separate male and female plants went up as latitude went down, that is, as we moved closer to the equator.

The share of monoecious species (both male and female parts on the same plant) and the share of dioecious species (separate male and female plants) showed opposite trends, and these trends differed strongly from region to region along the overall north–south gradient (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006). Overall, our results indicate that the share of monoecious species rises with latitude, while the share of dioecious species falls as latitude rises. To some extent, this suggests that the shares of monoecious and dioecious species may be closely linked to the region, especially to how far north it lies. The share of plants with both male and female parts on the same plant, however, showed no clear regular pattern along the latitude gradient (Chen and Li, 2008).

Early studies found more dioecious species than monoecious species in tropical regions near the equator (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also confirmed our finding that many tropical tree species that grow thinly scattered have a higher share of dioecious species. More recently, Wang et al. (2021) used nearly 70,000 species of flowering plants to study where each sexual system is found around the world. They confirmed that both dioecious and monoecious species are more common farther from the equator. Other studies have also found that dioecious species are more common farther from the equator in the Northern Hemisphere. Studies in North America and Siberia found that the share of dioecious species rises with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017).

The current worldwide pattern of sexual systems in flowering plants is due to dioecious and monoecious plants being able to cope with a wider range of conditions and to spread their seeds more widely. Our findings may also be relevant to the fact that our data were the first species counts for these large plots, and that they therefore agree with earlier studies by other researchers (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

4.2.

How climate affects the number of sexual systems

In the study of how plants reproduce, both sexual systems and the mating patterns they set up are very sensitive to changes in climate and in the landscape (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). Our results show that the link between plants with both male and female parts on the same plant and latitude, and between these plants and mean annual temperature (MAT, the average temperature over a year), is stronger than the link for monoecious and dioecious plants. For all three sexual systems, trees and shrubs had the strongest links with latitude and mean annual temperature (Figure 2).

Climate, meaning temperature and rainfall, can also affect which sexual system a plant shows. It does this by changing how plants work inside and how they live in their surroundings, and by affecting how well they reproduce while they are flowering (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). Our results suggest that, for all species together, for trees alone and for shrubs alone, the best models explaining the share of each of the three sexual systems picked out measures of temperature and rainfall (Figure 4).

Other factors may also affect how the share of each sexual system varies from place to place, for all species, for trees and for shrubs. These include the shape of the land, mean annual precipitation (MAP, the total rain and snow over a year), precipitation dryness measure (PDM, how dry a place is compared with how much water it can hold) and mean temperature of the coldest three months (MTCM). However, their effects were weaker than those of mean annual temperature and precipitation dryness measure (PWM). These findings suggest that climate should be the main driver of which sexual systems are present and how varied they are.

This may be because the climate is changing, for example with less rainfall and warmer winters, and because the timing of plants' yearly events is shifting, such as flowering earlier (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). Males and females also need different resources, such as water and nutrients. These differences further affect how populations are made up, which sexual systems are found in a local area, and even where sexual systems are found across the landscape (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Other findings support studies of what decides which species make up forest communities, at different scales (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study of how environmental stress affects the balance of male and female plants in flowering plants found a statistically significant link between the ratio of monoecious to dioecious species and climate factors (temperature and rainfall) (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). In short, our results confirm recent findings that temperature and rainfall are major drivers of where sexual systems are found in woody plant communities. They also suggest that the effects of place should not be ignored when we try to understand what shapes the mix of sexual systems.

Our results therefore suggest that sexual systems are not only features that evolve over long periods. They are also working ecological indicators: signs that bring together how plants reproduce and the conditions around them. Because sexual systems are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, keeping track of changes in how common monoecious and dioecious species are could give valuable clues about how forest communities are responding to ongoing climate change. This shows that plant sexual systems could be a new, feature-based way to monitor the variety of life as the world warms.

We also counted the number of species in each sexual system directly, rather than adjusting it for the total number of species in each plot. As a result, some of the patterns we saw across places may partly reflect differences in how many species each plot holds, as well as changes in the mix of sexual systems. Future studies that use counts adjusted for the total number of species, or measures of how common each sexual system is compared with the others, may help separate these effects.

4.3.

How non-living factors affect the number of sexual systems in trees and shrubs

Our structural equation model showed that the statistically significant links between climate and the shape of the land and the three sexual systems of trees were stronger than those for shrubs (Figure 4). This agrees with earlier large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Woody plants generally live longer and grow bigger. Their parts above the ground stay exposed to the climate for long periods, which may make them more sensitive to long-term changes in their surroundings (Wang et al., 2020a). So climate has a significant effect on where woody plants are found, compared with shrubs (Currie and Paquin, 1987).

These results suggest that climate may affect the spread of sexual systems differently in woody plants and in shrubs because the two growth forms have different ways of getting and using resources.

One limitation of this study is that we did not directly take into account how closely related the species are. Sexual systems are often passed down through a plant's family tree, so closely related plants may share similar ways of reproducing because they share a common history. Therefore, some of the patterns we saw across places may partly reflect differences in which family lines make up each forest community, or in how those communities came to be in the past, rather than only the effects of the environment. Future studies that include information on how species are related would help separate how much evolutionary history and how much the environment each contribute to large-scale differences in the sexual systems of woody plants.

4.4.

Could sexual systems help us keep watch on forests?

Our findings suggest that the mix of sexual systems, especially changes in the shares of dioecious and monoecious species, may be a useful feature-based sign of environmental conditions. Tracking changes in this mix may add useful information to long-term forest monitoring programs such as ForestGEO and CForBio. Because where each sexual system is found was significantly linked to climate, tracking changes in the mix may also add information about how forest communities respond to changes in their surroundings.

However, our study is based on links across places with different climates, not on observations over time. So it does not directly test how well sexual systems work as signs of ongoing climate change. Compared with traditional methods such as remote sensing, which often measure how green the treetops are or how much plant material there is, the mix of sexual systems may give extra insight into how plants reproduce and how communities come together. Even so, monitoring sexual systems over large areas needs long-term field observations and experts who can identify plants, which may limit how useful it is for quick assessments. Future studies that combine monitoring of sexual systems with remote sensing and databases of plant features may offer a more complete way to track how the variety of life responds to environmental change.

parts.title: How the way trees and shrubs reproduce changes with latitude, and what drives it, in forests across the Northern Hemisphere
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Introduction

A plant's way of reproducing, its sexual system, is one of the most important features that shape how forests grow and change, and how those forests evolve. Yet we still do not understand well how this system varies from place to place as you move from the equator toward the poles.

Methods

We gathered records of 3,595 kinds of woody plants (plants with wood, such as trees and shrubs) from 30 large forest monitoring plots. These plots cover tropical, subtropical and temperate regions across the Northern Hemisphere. We then looked for large-scale patterns in three statistical methods. Linear regression tests how one thing changes along with another. Redundancy analysis tests how much of the differences between plots can be linked to a set of environmental factors. Structural equation modeling tests a whole network of possible cause-and-effect paths at once.

Results

The share of species that grow with both male and female flowers on the same plant (monoecious species) rose as we moved toward the poles. The share of species with separate male and female flowers on different plants (dioecious species) fell. These two groups therefore show opposite trends. Climate, especially temperature and rainfall, was the main driver of these patterns. The links between climate and the way plants reproduce were stronger in trees than in shrubs.

Discussion

Our results show that differences in how woody plants reproduce from place to place are closely tied to changes in climate. The share of monoecious and dioecious species changed in the same way as conditions changed. This shows that the way plants reproduce matters for how forests work. It also suggests that these patterns may give useful clues, based on plant features, for understanding how forest communities respond to a changing environment. More long-term studies are needed to judge whether they could be useful for keeping watch on forests as the climate keeps changing.

Keywords: climate change, ecological indicator (a feature that shows how a place is doing), latitudinal gradient (how conditions change with distance from the equator), sexual systems, woody plants
parts.introduction_first:
As you move from the equator toward the poles, the number of different species on Earth goes down. This is one of the most important patterns in the history of life on Earth, and it shows up in forests in every climate zone (Rosenzweig, 1995).

A flower is one of a plant's reproductive organs, and it is part of the plant's whole system for making seeds. Scientists sort plants' sexual systems into three groups: monoecious, dioecious and some more complex systems (Cardoso et al., 2018; Yampolsky and Yampolsky, 1922). In a monoecious plant, both male and female flowers grow on the same plant. In a dioecious plant, the male and female flowers grow on different plants. In a more complex system, both kinds of flower sit on the same plant.

The way a plant reproduces affects how it breeds. That, in turn, affects the genetic makeup of its populations and the direction in which those populations are evolving (Barrett, 1992; Fox, 1985; Sabath et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020a). So sexual systems play an important part in building and keeping up plant communities and whole ecosystems (Chen and Li, 2008; Ibarra‐Manríquez and Oyama, 1992).

Sexual systems do more than show how plants respond to a changing environment. They also shape how forests evolve across a whole region (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Charlesworth, 2006; Campbell and Kessler, 2013). Earlier studies have shown strong changes in plant variety and in which plants make up a community as you move from the equator toward the poles. These changes differ a lot between regions such as East Asia and North America (Boufford and Spongberg, 1983; Wang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2017).

Most of these studies, however, looked at how many species there are, how many different kinds of plants there are, or at plant features such as size and shape. Much less attention has gone to how the way plants reproduce varies across whole communities. Among these features, sexual systems play a basic role in how plants reproduce, how their populations rise and fall, and how they evolve.

Even so, we still know little about large-scale patterns in how woody plants reproduce across the world, especially in forests that mix tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. This gap limits what we can learn about how the way plants reproduce changes with climate, and how it responds to a changing environment.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We mapped how often each of the three ways of reproducing (monoecious, dioecious and more complex) turned up across 30 communities in different regions, and we compared how non-living parts of the environment, such as climate, affect how often each way of reproducing appears.

We found that the share of monoecious and dioecious plants changed as we moved from the equator toward the poles. Trees and shrubs differed in a statistically significant way in how often their sexual systems appeared and in what shaped them. (A result is called statistically significant when a difference this large would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no difference.) These findings show how the way forests reproduce relates to their environment as you move from the equator toward the poles.

Taken together, our study reveals large-scale patterns in how woody plants reproduce across the world. It also shows that these patterns can be used as practical ecological indicators, meaning features that show how a place is doing, for judging and predicting how ecosystems will change as the climate changes. Adding changes in sexual systems to long-term forest monitoring may greatly improve our ability to spot, understand and reduce the effects of climate change on the variety of life on Earth.
parts.introduction_rest:
Recent evidence suggests that the way plants reproduce varies from place to place is shaped by many things at once. These include a plant's life form (for example, a tree or a shrub), its reproductive traits, its climate, and the history of how it grew up (Chazdon et al., 2003; Queenborough et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2020b). Scientists often use latitudinal gradients, the way conditions change with distance from the equator, to study large-scale patterns in nature. This is because they are closely tied to steady changes in climate, such as temperature and rainfall.

However, latitude is not a direct cause of these patterns. Instead, it stands in for several other environmental conditions that change across space. Climate may directly affect how a plant's reproduction develops, when it flowers, and how it shares out its resources. In this way, climate may affect where different ways of reproducing occur and where they are found (Barrett and Harder, 1996; Gougherty and Gougherty, 2018; Inouye et al., 2019). Stress from the environment, such as drought or extreme temperatures, may also change how a plant shows up as male or female and how much it invests in reproduction. It can do this by affecting how well the plant's body works and how plants interact with one another in nature (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Hultine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2021; Petry et al., 2016). For example, conditions may change how much the costs and benefits of male and female reproduction are compared with each other. They may also change how well pollination works, or how plants share out their resources between growing and reproducing. In the end, these processes can shape where different ways of reproducing occur and how long they last within plant communities.

So the way plants reproduce varies from place to place may reflect both large-scale latitudinal patterns and the environmental conditions that go along with them.

Different environmental conditions reflect differences in how varied a habitat is and how much food and other resources it offers.
