Because latitude brings together many climate and ecological factors, it is a good way to study large-scale patterns in plant features. Earlier studies have shown that features linked to how plants reproduce change in a regular way as conditions change (Bleher et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2020b; Xia et al., 2020). Even so, we still know very little about whether the way woody plants reproduce follows the same geographic pattern across forests in tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. Answering this question will help us understand how the way plants reproduce responds to changes in their environment across large areas.

The link between the way plants reproduce and the type of plant growth has received the most attention (Renner, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Earlier studies have confirmed that features linked to sexual systems, such as life style, how old a plant's family tree is, and seed quality, are spread out along environmental gradients (Moles, 2018; Stephen, 1992). So the way plants reproduce may also follow some kind of geographic pattern as resources change.

One study looked at 491 genera of flowering plants (Vamosi et al., 2003). It found that dioecious plants were more closely linked to woody life forms, especially trees, than monoecious plants were. Studies that compared temperate forests in Sri Lanka and in our own country have also confirmed this link (Senarath, 2008; Renner, 2014; Wang et al., 2018). Another study looked at 19,780 flowering plants in China (Wang et al., 2020a). It showed that woody and non-woody plants differed in how often each way of reproducing appeared. It also showed that the share of different drivers, especially climate, how old a plant's family tree was, and how tall the plants were when they mature, varied between growth forms.

Woody plants generally have taller canopies (the leafy tops of the trees), live longer, and put more resources into reproduction than non-woody plants. This makes them more likely to build up genetic changes over time. Differences in how fast they evolve may therefore help explain why woody and non-woody plants evolve in different ways in response to climate (Renner and Ricklefs, 1995; Renner, 2014).

Within woody plants, trees and shrubs also differ a great deal in how tall their canopies are, how long they live, how they gather resources, and how they share out their reproduction. These differences may lead to different responses in which ways of reproducing are common as conditions change. So studying where sexual systems occur in trees and shrubs, and what drives them, will help us understand large-scale patterns in how plants reproduce.

In this study, we used records of where sexual systems occur in 3,595 species of woody plants from 30 forest communities. We looked for large-scale trends in how woody plants reproduce, and in the main environmental factors that drive them, as you move from the equator toward the poles.

The climate and environmental conditions change in different ways from low latitudes to high latitudes. The 30 forest communities we chose range from humid to dry climates, from high plateaus to low-lying plains, and from cold temperate zones, where the seasons are cold, to tropical climates and high-lying land in the south. This range lets us study how vegetation patterns change across a wide range of environmental conditions.

In general, we set out to answer three questions. (1) How do the ways plants reproduce change with latitude across the 30 forest communities? (2) How do the places where different ways of reproducing occur respond to environmental factors? (3) Do trees and shrubs show similar patterns in how often each way of reproducing occurs as you move from the equator toward the poles, and what are the main environmental factors linked to these patterns?
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

Where we studied

Over the past thirty years, the Forest Global Earth Observatory has been working on long-term, large-scale forest data for tropical, subtropical and temperate forests (ForestGEO; https://forestgeo.si.edu/what-forestgeo) (Condit, 1995). The Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network (CForBio) (http://www.cfbiodiv.org) has also grown the CTFS network, a set of monitoring plots that follow forests over many years. It has set up large mapping plots along the range of latitudes, from the equator toward the poles, in temperate, subtropical and tropical forests. Altogether, we had 20 plots from ForestGEO and ten from CForBio. The two sets of plots are independent of each other and do not overlap.

All of our study plots were large forest monitoring plots, each covering at least 20 hectares (a hectare is a square 100 meters on each side). We focused on forests in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, there were few long-term forest monitoring plots with complete information on how the plants reproduce.

In this study, we compared the way woody plants reproduce across a range of latitudes in 30 forest communities from the two networks (Figure 1a). The plots lie between 0.2918° N and 61.3000° N, at heights of 56 to 1902 meters above sea level. The number of species ranges from 11 to 408, and some of these plots are among the forests with the most species in the world (for example, Xishuangbanna) (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2025). These big differences in climate and geography affect how the way plants reproduce changes from plot to plot.

Every plot we used had at least 1 cm of trunk measured at chest height (diameter at breast height, or DBH). We looked only at trees and shrubs and left out other kinds of growth, such as woody climbing vines (lianas) and palms.

Figure 1

The 30 forest plots around the world. They range from 20 hectares (Xishuangbanna) to 120 hectares (Mpala). They stretch from 0.2918° N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3° N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and they cover forests on Asia, Europe and North America (a). The number of species in each way of reproducing in each forest community (b). A map of how similar the communities are, made with a method called NMDS (c).

2.2.

Data on how plants reproduce and on the environment

We gathered information on 3595 species from the 30 permanent monitoring plots. Records can be wrong because they are made at different times, in different regions and by different researchers. To remove these errors, we checked the species names in every community against the Flora of the Republic of China (1959–2004) and eFloras (http://efloras.org/). We checked the species recorded by different sources again and again and corrected any that did not agree.

The way a species reproduces can change with local living and non-living conditions, such as climate or how many pollinators are around (Barrett and Harder, 2017) (e.g. Schoen, 1982). For this reason, we left out species whose sexual system was not the same everywhere. Based on the type of plant, we split the data into two groups: trees and shrubs.

We built the list of ways these woody plants reproduce from three sources: Flora of China (http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2, accessed in May 2020), eFloras and Tree of Sex (Ashman et al., 2014). Following Cardoso et al. (2018), we sorted the species into three groups.

Hermaphroditic species have both male and female flowers in the same flower. Dioecious species have male and female flowers on different plants. This includes androdioecy, where male and female flowers grow on the same plant, and gynodioecy, where they grow on different plants. Trioecy is a more complex form of this. Monoecious species have male and female flowers on the same plant. This includes andromonoecy, where male and female flowers grow on the same plant, and gynomonoecy, where they grow on different plants.

For each plot, we took the longitude and latitude. We also took the shape of the land: the average slope (MS, in degrees), the average height above sea level (ME, in meters), the highest point (HA, in meters) and the lowest point (LE, in meters). Finally, we took climate: the average yearly rainfall (MAP, in millimeters), the rainfall in the wettest month (PWM, in millimeters per month), the rainfall in the driest month (PDM, in millimeters per month), the average yearly temperature (MAT, in °C), and the average temperature of the warmest month (MTWM, in °C) and the coldest month (MTCM, in °C).

The latitude, longitude and land-shape data came from ForestGEO (https://forestgeo.si.edu/) and the Chinese Forest Biodiversity Monitoring Network. For plots where these sources did not give land-shape data, we used land-shape data from the monitoring network's own maps. We calculated these values using the methods of Harms et al. (2001) and Valencia et al. (2004). The climate data came from ForestGEO or from published studies (Anderson-Teixeira et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2024).

For each forest plot, we measured the way plants reproduce in two ways that complement each other. First, we worked out the share of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. This showed how the mix of ways of reproducing changes from place to place (Figure 1). Second, we counted how many species of each way of reproducing each plot had. This let us test how the variety of ways of reproducing relates to latitude, climate and land-shape (Figure 2).

Figure 2

How the number of species relates to different features of woody plants' way of reproducing in the 30 plots. The left column shows a spatial linear model, a statistical method that tests how one thing changes along with others. Here, the number of species was the outcome, and climate, land-shape and latitude were the possible causes. The right column shows the same model with the errors left unexplained. The three rows from right to left are all species, then trees, then shrubs. The five columns from top to bottom are the average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average height above sea level (ME) and average slope (MS).

2.3.

How we analyzed the data

We chose five environmental factors: latitude, average yearly temperature (MAT), average yearly rainfall (MAP), average height above sea level (ME) and average slope (MS). Earlier studies have shown that climate, especially temperature and rainfall, and the unevenness of the land, are major drivers of how plants reproduce and which plants make up a community.

We worked out the share of each way of reproducing in each of the 30 forest communities from the species records in that community. To show how the mix of ways of reproducing differs between climate zones, we drew alluvial diagrams. These are maps made with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020), in which each species is a dot, and dots that sit close together have similar mixes of ways of reproducing. We also drew graphs showing how the number of species differs between the three ways of reproducing.

We used non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) to compare the communities. NMDS draws a kind of map in which points stand for the communities, and the closer two points are, the more alike their communities are. The distance between points shows how different the places are (Chen et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2022). To judge how well the NMDS fits the data, and whether the ranking makes sense, we used a measure called the stress coefficient. In this study, we ranked how many woody plants each of the 30 plots had on the NMDS map. We then drew circles around the communities in each climate zone to show how their mix of ways of reproducing differs.

We used linear regression to explore how latitude and the environmental factors relate to the way woody plants reproduce. The outcome was the number of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. The possible causes were latitude, average yearly temperature, average yearly rainfall, average height above sea level and average slope. We counted species as absolute richness, meaning the actual number of species, rather than as a share of all species in the plot. We did not adjust the numbers for the total number of species in the plot.

Some of our factors may rise and fall together, which can confuse a model. To check for this, we used a measure called the variance inflation factor (VIF) (Supplementary Table 1). All VIF values were below 10, which means the factors were not too closely linked to each other.

We used the model-adjusted R² to show how much of the variation in species turnover (Tang et al., 2012) the environmental factors and the factors on species turnover could explain. Species turnover is the change in which species are present as you move from one place to another. With so many factors, a model can end up overestimating the results. To avoid this, we compared two versions of the model. One used the sample information criterion, a score that rewards a model for fitting the data well without being needlessly complicated. We kept the best version for the environmental factors and the best version for the spatial factors.

Redundancy analysis (RDA) is a ranking method that combines regression analysis with principal component analysis (Borcard et al., 1992; Smith and Lundholm, 2010; Xi et al., 2021). In this analysis, the outcome was the number of species in each of the three ways of reproducing. The possible causes were longitude and latitude, the land-shape factors (average slope, average height above sea level, highest point and lowest point), and the climate factors (average yearly rainfall, rainfall in the wettest month, rainfall in the driest month, average yearly temperature, average temperature of the warmest month and average temperature of the coldest month). We used the "envfit" function to test how the environmental factors affect where the woody plant communities are found. To do this, we shuffled the environmental data 999 times and compared the real pattern with the shuffled ones.

We also wanted to compare how the non-living factors (latitude, land shape and climate) affect where the ways of reproducing are found. For this, we built a structural equation model (SEM). We assumed that the total effect of the non-living factors on where the ways of reproducing are found acts directly on it. We also assumed that latitude, average yearly temperature, rainfall in the wettest month, average temperature of the warmest month and average slope act directly or indirectly on it.

The SEM is a statistical method based on regression models (Grace, 2006). It has two parts. The inner part (the internal model) links the possible causes to one another. The outer part (the external model) links the observed outcomes to the possible causes. In this study, the possible cause was the number of species in each way of reproducing, and the observed outcome was the environmental factors. The model also included the way the numbers of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species vary together. These three groups of species together describe the mix of ways of reproducing in a community, and they are not statistically independent of each other. Arrows that point in both directions show that two things vary together, not that one causes the other.

We ran all analyses in R 4.0.3 (R Core Development Team2). We made the alluvial plots with the "ggalluvial" package (Brunson, 2020), and we ran the NMDS and RDA with the "vegan" package (Oksanen et al., 2010). We ran the SEM with the "lavaan" package (Rosseel Y et al., 2012).

Results

3.1.

A pattern of ways of reproducing that changes with latitude

We looked at how the way woody plants reproduce was spread across 30 forest monitoring plots. The plots covered tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. In most plots, the share of monoecious species rose as we moved toward the poles. The share of hermaphroditic species (plants with both male and female flowers on the same plant) showed the opposite pattern. The share of dioecious species (plants with separate male and female flowers on different plants) stayed fairly steady along the line from equator to pole (Figure 1b).

These trends suggest that the mix of ways of reproducing changes in a regular way from one climate zone to another.

To see which species made up each plot, we used a method called NMDS. It draws a kind of map in which plots with similar species sit close together and plots with different species sit far apart. The NMDS analysis showed statistically significant differences in which species were present among the 30 forest communities (Bray–Curtis stress = 0.031; Figure 1c). Bray–Curtis stress is a score of how well the map fits the real differences between plots, and a lower score means a better fit.

Panel a of Figure 1 shows where the 30 forest plots lie. They stretch from 0.29°N (Mpala, Republic of the Congo) to 61.3°N (Scotty Creek, Canada), and the plots range in size from 20 hectares to 120 hectares. Panel b shows, for each climate zone, the share of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic species. Panel c shows how the species mix differs among the forest communities, based on the NMDS map.

We included only plots in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, we had few long-term forest monitoring plots with complete information on the way plants reproduce.

3.2.

How non-living parts of the environment affect how often each way of reproducing appears

We first asked how the number of species in each way of reproducing was linked to latitude and to mean annual temperature (MAT), which is the average temperature over a year. For each link we report an R²adj value. This number shows how much of the variation in the number of species lines up with latitude and temperature, on a scale from 0 (none) to 1 (all of it).

For plants as a whole, trees and shrubs together, the number of species was linked fairly strongly with latitude and mean annual temperature. The R²adj values were 0.413 for plants as a whole, 0.511 for trees and 0.412 for shrubs. The share of monoecious species was linked much less strongly with these two factors (0.181 for plants as a whole, 0.412 for trees and 0.100 for shrubs). The share of dioecious species was linked less strongly (0.353 for plants as a whole, 0.419 for trees and 0.310 for shrubs) (Figure 2).

The number of monoecious and dioecious species was also significantly linked with mean annual temperature, but not with latitude. For monoecious plants, the link with temperature was stronger than the link with latitude (R²adj = 0.421 compared with 0.181, P < 0.001). For dioecious plants, the link with temperature was stronger than the link with latitude (R²adj = 0.544 compared with 0.343, P < 0.005).

The number of species in all three ways of reproducing was significantly negatively linked with latitude: where it was higher, the plots were closer to the equator. It was significantly positively linked with mean annual temperature (Figure 2).

We also looked at the different kinds of plants. For trees and shrubs, the number of species was most strongly linked with latitude and mean annual temperature. It was next most strongly linked with mean annual precipitation (MAP), which is the total rain and snow in a year, and least strongly linked with slope (how steep the ground is) and mean elevation (the average height of the land). The links with mean elevation and mean slope were generally weak compared with the links to climate. Even so, we found some significant links in particular ways of reproducing and in particular kinds of plants (Figures 2d, e).

Next, we asked how much of the differences in the mix of ways of reproducing could be linked to the environment. For monoecious plants, the environment explained 7.57% of these differences. For dioecious plants, it explained 8.45%, and for hermaphroditic plants, 7.37%.

We then used redundancy analysis to find which environmental factors mattered most. Longitude and mean annual temperature were the most important factors for all three ways of reproducing. Precipitation in the wettest month (PWM) was also an important factor for all three. For trees and shrubs, the most important factors were climate and longitude, respectively (Figure 3).

Figure 3

Redundancy analysis (RDA) maps of the mix of monoecious, dioecious and hermaphroditic communities for each kind of plant. The ellipses show the 95% confidence region, the area where the true pattern is likely to lie. “*” marks a link with the environment (P < 0.05), “**” marks a strong link (P < 0.01) and “***” marks a very strong link (P < 0.001). MS, mean slope; ME, mean elevation; HA, highest elevation; LE, lowest elevation; MAP, mean annual precipitation; PWM, precipitation of the wettest month; PDM, precipitation of the driest month; MAT, mean annual temperature; MTWM, mean temperature of the warmest month; MTCM, mean temperature of the coldest month.

3.3.

How climate affects how often each way of reproducing appears

We used structural equation modeling to test a whole network of possible cause-and-effect paths at once. In this model, climate factors (mean annual temperature, mean temperature of the warmest month and precipitation in the wettest month) were positively linked with the number of species in all three ways of reproducing.

We also measured how strong each path was, using a number called a path coefficient. A larger number means a stronger link. For monoecious plants, the path coefficient was 0.88. For dioecious plants it was 0.70, and for hermaphroditic plants it was 0.77. All three values were higher than for the three ways of reproducing linked to the shape of the land and to space (Figure 4).

The kinds of plants also differed. For dioecious trees, the path coefficient for climate was lower (0.88) than for shrubs (0.96). For dioecious shrubs, it was higher (0.81) than for trees (0.75). For hermaphroditic flowers, it was higher (0.90) than for trees (0.57) (Figure 4).

These results show that the different ways of reproducing respond to the environment in different ways. The monoecious way of reproducing was more strongly linked to the environment than the dioecious way.

Figure 4

The number next to each arrow is the path coefficient, put on a common scale so that arrows of different sizes can be compared. Red arrows show negative links (one thing goes down as the other goes up) and blue arrows show positive links. Wider arrows mean stronger links. “***” marks a path with P < 0.001, “**” marks a path with P < 0.01 and “*” marks a path with P < 0.05.

4.

Discussion

We found a clear pattern: the number of species in each of the three ways of reproducing changed with latitude, that is, with distance from the equator, in different forest communities from region to region. These large-scale patterns differed between the three groups of plants and between trees and shrubs. Climate explained a large share of this variation.

4.1.

How the variety of plant ways of reproducing changes with latitude

We compared the share of each way of reproducing in forests across latitudes in the tropics, the subtropics and the temperate zones. In East Asia and North America, the share of hermaphrodite species (plants with both male and female flowers on the same plant) did not rise or fall significantly as we moved from the equator toward the poles. The share of dioecious species, which have separate male and female flowers on different plants, did rise as we moved toward the poles.

The two groups of plants followed opposite trends, and this creates strong differences from place to place along the whole latitude gradient (Ramírez, 2005; Ramirez and Brito, 1990; MaChado et al., 2006). Overall, our results show that the share of monoecious species rises in step with latitude, while the share of dioecious species falls as you move toward the poles. To some extent, this suggests that the share of monoecious and dioecious species may be closely linked to the region, especially to latitude. However, the share of hermaphrodite plants showed no obvious regular pattern along the latitude gradient (Chen and Li, 2008).

Early studies found more dioecious species than monoecious species in tropical regions at low latitudes (Freeman et al., 1979; Sakai et al., 1995; Matallana et al., 2005). Nathan and Muller (2000) also confirmed our findings: many tropical trees that grow in thin, scattered stands have a higher share of dioecious species. More recently, Wang et al. (2021) used nearly 70,000 species of flowering plants to explore how sexual systems are spread across the world. Their work confirmed that both dioecious and monoecious species are more common at high latitudes. Other studies have found that dioecious species are more common at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere. Studies in North America and Siberia have also found that the share of dioecious species rises with latitude (Fox, 1985; Freeman et al., 1979; Godin, 2014; Kevan and Godglick, 2017).

The way sexual systems are spread across the world today is due to two things: dioecious and monoecious plants can cope with a wider range of conditions, and they are better at spreading to new places. Our findings may also be relevant to a fact about our data. These were the first species counts for these large plots, so they agree with earlier studies by others (Chen and Li, 2008; Nathan and Muller, 2000; Gross, 2005).

4.2.

How climate affects the number of species in each way of reproducing

In the study of how plants reproduce, the way plants reproduce, and the mating patterns it sets, are very sensitive to changes in climate and in the places they grow (Hedhly et al., 2009; Eckert et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2011). Our results show that the link between hermaphrodite plants and latitude is stronger than the link between monoecious plants and dioecious plants. Trees and shrubs of all three groups were also most strongly linked to latitude and to temperature and rainfall (Figure 2).

Climate, meaning temperature and rainfall, can also shape how common each way of reproducing is. It does this by changing how plants' bodies work and how they live, and by controlling how well they reproduce during flowering (Charlesworth, 2006; Weeks et al., 2014). Our results suggest that the environmental temperature and rainfall factors we chose in the best models explained the share of species in all three groups, for trees and for shrubs (Figure 4).

The shape of the land, the average yearly rainfall, the amount of plant material that plants can store (called PDM), and the total amount of carbon they take in (called MTCM) may also affect how the share of each way of reproducing varies from place to place. These factors may affect all species, trees and shrubs separately. However, their effects are weaker than those of temperature and rainfall and of the amount of carbon plants take in. These findings suggest that climate should be the main driver of which ways of reproducing are present and how varied they are. This may be due to ongoing climate changes, such as less rainfall and warmer winters, and to changes in the timing of plant events, such as flowering (Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Liu et al., 2021). Differences in how much each way of reproducing needs from plants, such as how many flowers they need, also affect how populations are made up and how the variety of ways of reproducing is spread out locally and across the world (Kay and Picklum, 2013; Etterson and Mazer, 2016; Wang et al., 2020b).

Other findings confirm studies of what shapes which species make up forest communities, at different scales (Ramírez, 2005; Wang et al., 2020b, 2021). For example, a recent study of how environmental stress affects the balance of male and female flowers in flowering plants found a statistically significant link between the share of monoecious and dioecious species and climate factors (temperature and rainfall) (Varga and Soulsbury, 2020). In short, our results confirm recent findings that temperature and rainfall are major drivers of where woody plants reproduce. They also suggest that the effects of place should not be ignored when we try to understand what shapes which ways of reproducing are present.

Our results therefore suggest that ways of reproducing are not just inherited features. They are also ecological indicators, meaning features that bring together how plants reproduce and the conditions around them. Because they are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, keeping track of changes in the share of monoecious and dioecious species could give useful clues about how forest communities are responding to ongoing climate change. This shows that the way plants reproduce could become a new, feature-based way to keep watch on the variety of life as the world warms.

We also looked at the number of species in each group of ways of reproducing, without first adjusting it for the total number of species in each plot. As a result, some of the patterns we see may partly reflect differences in how varied the whole community is from plot to plot, as well as changes in which ways of reproducing are present. Future studies that use measures adjusted for the total number of species, or that measure how common each way of reproducing is compared with the others, may help untangle these effects.

4.3.

How non-living parts of the environment affect the number of species in each way of reproducing

Our structural equation model showed that climate and the shape of the land had statistically significant links with the three ways of reproducing in trees, but stronger links with trees than with shrubs (Figure 4). This agrees with earlier large-scale studies (Oberle et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Woody plants generally live longer and grow larger. Their parts above the ground stay exposed to the weather for a long time, which may make them more sensitive to long-term changes in their environment (Wang et al., 2020a). For these reasons, climate has a significant effect on where woody plants grow compared with where shrubs grow (Currie and Paquin, 1987). These results suggest that the different effects of climate on woody and shrub species may also be linked to how the two groups of plants get and use resources, such as light, water and nutrients, in different ways.

One limitation of our study is that we did not directly include how closely related the species are through evolution. The ways plants reproduce are often passed down from one generation to the next, and closely related groups may share similar ways of reproducing because they share a common evolutionary history. So some of the patterns we see may partly reflect differences in which lines of descent are present, or in how species were spread across the land in the past, rather than only the environment filtering which species can live there. Future studies that include evolutionary relationships would help untangle how much evolutionary history and how much the environment each contribute to large-scale differences in woody plants' ways of reproducing.

4.4.

How useful the way plants reproduce could be for monitoring

Our findings suggest that the mix of ways of reproducing, especially changes in the share of dioecious and monoecious species, may be a useful feature-based indicator of environmental conditions. Keeping track of changes in this mix may add to the information that long-term forest monitoring programs such as ForestGEO and CForBio.B provide. Because the spread of each way of reproducing was significantly linked to climate factors, tracking changes in the mix may also give clues about how forest communities respond to changes in their environment.

However, our study looks at how the ways of reproducing are linked across latitudes, not at changes over time. So it does not directly test how well the ways of reproducing work as indicators of ongoing climate change. Compared with traditional methods such as remote sensing (gathering information from satellites and aircraft), which often focuses on how green the treetops are or how much plant material there is, the mix of ways of reproducing may give extra insight into how plants reproduce and how communities come together. Nevertheless, keeping watch on ways of reproducing across large areas needs long-term field observations and experts who know how to identify plants, and this may limit its use for quick assessments. Future studies that combine tracking of ways of reproducing with remote sensing and databases of plant features may offer a fuller way to follow how the variety of life responds to environmental change.
